title: Stored energy: twice the pull-back stores more than twice the energy, but twice the height stores only twice

summary.text: Pull a rubber band back 2 centimetres and let go, and a bar of soap slides a short way. Pull it back 4 centimetres, twice as far, and the soap slides far more than twice as far. Yet a ball dropped from twice the height bounces only twice as high. A stretched band and a lifted ball both hold energy, and each kind of store fills up in its own way. In this unit you measure both, find out what lets stored energy out, and trace it back to where it first came from.
summary.art: A bar of soap on a tiled floor in front of two pencils standing in lumps of clay with a rubber band stretched between them, and a measuring tape laid beside the soap.

intro.hook: Stand two pencils in clay with a rubber band round them. Put a bar of soap against the band, and pull the soap back 2 centimetres. Let go, and the soap slides away. Now pull it back 4 centimetres, twice as far. How far will it slide?
intro.text: Most people guess twice as far. Try it and see. Before you let go, the pulled band was holding energy. Energy that is held like this is called stored energy, and the thing that holds it is called a store. A longer pull put more energy in. In this unit you measure how much more, for a band and for a lifted ball. You also find out what holds stored energy in place, where it first came from, and why a ball bounces lower every time.
intro.art: A child kneeling on a tiled floor pulling a bar of soap back against a stretched rubber band between two pencils, with a ruler beside it.

outcomes: I can name three kinds of store, which are height, stretch or squash, and chemical, and say what lets each one out.
I can explain that a store waits because something holds it back, and that a trigger lets it go.
I can use my own tests to explain why twice the height stores twice the energy, but twice the pull-back stores more than twice.
I can explain why a bouncing ball rises less each time, and where the missing energy has gone.
I can trace the energy in a dosa or in a full water tank back to the Sun, and name a store that does not come from the Sun.
I can explain why the energy a ball stores depends on how far it can fall, and not only on the ball.
I can use the joule as a unit, and compare a store of height with a store in food or a battery.

terms.meaning: Energy that is waiting inside a thing, ready to be used later. It waits because of where things are, or how they are shaped or joined.
terms.example: A rubber band pulled back and held is full of stored energy.
terms.art: A hand holding a rubber band pulled back between two pencils.

terms.meaning: The scientific name for stored energy. Potential means able to happen, so potential energy is energy that is able to be used.
terms.example: A coconut high on a palm has potential energy.
terms.art: A coconut hanging high on a palm tree against the sky.

terms.meaning: The scientific name for the energy of movement. Anything that is moving has kinetic energy, and the faster it moves, the more it has.
terms.example: A cricket ball flying through the air has kinetic energy.
terms.art: A cricket ball flying through the air with short speed lines behind it.

terms.meaning: The energy stored in height. When you lift a thing against the pull of the Earth, you store energy that comes out again when the thing falls.
terms.example: Water in a tank on a roof has gravitational potential energy.
terms.art: A black water tank on a flat roof with a pipe running down the side of the building.

terms.meaning: The energy stored when you stretch, squash, bend or twist something that springs back, such as a band or a spring.
terms.example: A bent bow holds elastic potential energy until the string is let go.
terms.art: A wooden bow bent back with an arrow, held by a hand.

terms.meaning: The energy stored in how atoms are joined together. Food, fuel and the chemicals in a battery all hold it.
terms.example: A banana holds chemical energy that your body can use.
terms.art: A banana, a small log and a battery cell in a row on a table.

terms.meaning: The small thing that lets a store release its energy. Until it happens, something holds the energy back.
terms.example: Opening a tap is the trigger that lets the water in a roof tank run down.
terms.art: A hand turning a tap on a pipe, with water starting to flow.

terms.meaning: The unit scientists use to measure energy. Lifting a small apple up by 1 metre stores about 1 joule.
terms.example: Lifting a bag of 2 apples up by 1 metre stores about 2 joules.
terms.art: A hand lifting a small apple one metre above a table beside a metre stick.

terms.meaning: A unit used for the energy in food. One kilocalorie is about 4200 joules. Food labels often say Calories or kcal for a kilocalorie.
terms.example: A medium banana holds about 100 kilocalories.
terms.art: The side of a food packet showing the energy in kilocalories for one serving.

terms.meaning: Squeezed into less space. Compressed air pushes back, because its tiny particles hit the walls more often when there is less room.
terms.example: The air in a bicycle pump is compressed when you push the handle down.
terms.art: A bicycle pump with the handle pushed down and an arrow showing air squeezed in the barrel.

terms.meaning: A battery that can be filled again. A charger pushes the chemical change in the battery backwards, so the chemical energy is stored again.
terms.example: A phone battery is rechargeable, and an ordinary torch cell is not.
terms.art: A phone plugged into a charger with a battery symbol that is filling.

terms.meaning: A way of storing electricity by pumping water uphill. Later the water runs down through turbines and makes electricity again.
terms.example: A dam at Kadamparai in Tamil Nadu pumps water uphill when electricity is plentiful.
terms.art: Two lakes on a hillside, one high and one low, joined by a pipe with a power house in between.

terms.meaning: How much of the energy you put into a machine comes out as the useful kind. The rest is lost, mostly as heat.
terms.example: A pumped storage dam gives back about three-quarters of the energy it was given.
terms.art: A bar split into a large useful part and a small lost part shown as wavy heat lines.

explanations.concept: Stored energy: energy that waits because of where things are or how they are joined
explanations.definition: Stored energy, which scientists call potential energy, is energy that a thing holds because of its place or its shape, and that can be turned into movement later.
explanations.description: A lifted ball is not moving, yet it can fall. A pulled-back band is not moving, yet it can spring. A banana is not moving, yet it can power you for a long walk. In each, energy is waiting. There are three stores you meet most. Energy can wait in height. It can wait in a stretch, a squash, a bend or a twist. And it can wait in how atoms are joined, which is called chemical energy. When a store lets go, its energy turns into movement energy, which scientists call kinetic energy. The amount that waits is the amount that can come out.
examples: A coconut high on a palm holds energy in height.
A bent bow holds energy in a bend.
A banana holds chemical energy.
A lit torch cell turns its chemical energy into light.
explanations.art: Three objects in a row, a ball held high, a bent bow and a banana, each with a small label saying what kind of store it is.

explanations.concept: Energy stored in height: twice as high, or twice as heavy, stores twice as much
explanations.definition: The energy stored in height is the weight of the thing times the height it was lifted. Twice the height stores twice the energy, and twice the weight stores twice the energy.
explanations.description: To lift a thing, you pull against the Earth's pull, and the energy you spend is stored. The scientists' unit is the joule. Lifting a small apple, which weighs about 100 grams, up by 1 metre stores about 1 joule. Lifting it 2 metres stores 2 joules. Lifting 2 apples 1 metre also stores 2 joules. A full roof tank of 1000 litres, lifted 10 metres, holds about 98 000 joules. When a thing falls, the stored energy turns into movement. A thing dropped from twice the height hits harder. The Bounce Ratio test shows that a ball dropped from twice the height also comes back up twice as high.
examples: A 1000 litre tank on a roof 10 metres up holds about 98 000 joules.
A child at the top of a slide stores more energy than one halfway up.
A coconut falls from the top of a tall palm with more energy than from a low one.
explanations.art: Two apples lifted to one metre and two metres on a measuring stick, with a label of one joule and two joules.

explanations.concept: Energy stored in a stretch or a squash: it grows faster than the stretch
explanations.definition: When a spring or a band is pulled further, the energy it stores grows faster than the pull. For a good spring, twice the stretch stores four times the energy.
explanations.description: Pull a rubber band slowly and feel it. The first centimetre is easy. The last centimetre is hard. The band pulls back harder the more you stretch it, so every extra centimetre costs more energy than the one before. Stretch a band twice as far, and you pull twice as hard at the end, over twice the distance. Twice as hard over twice as far is 2 times 2, which is 4. That is why twice the pull-back stores more than twice the energy. The English scientist Robert Hooke published in 1678 that, for a spring, the pull grows in step with the stretch. From that, scientists work out that the stored energy grows with the stretch multiplied by itself. Real rubber bands follow this only roughly, and a stretched band also warms up a little. Air works like a spring too. When you squash air into less room, it pushes back harder.
examples: A bow drawn back twice as far sends the arrow much faster.
A squashed spring on a pen stores more energy the further you press the button.
A bicycle pump gets harder to push as the air inside is squeezed.
explanations.art: A rubber band stretched three steps against a ruler, with arrows getting longer to show the pull back growing stronger.

explanations.concept: A store waits only while something holds it back, and the trigger lets it go
explanations.definition: A trigger is the small thing that lets a store release its energy. A store stays full as long as something holds the energy back.
explanations.description: A stretched band waits because your fingers hold it. A tank of water waits because a closed tap holds it. A heap of firewood waits for years in air that is full of oxygen, because it needs a little heat to get started. A battery waits because the circuit is open, so its chemicals cannot react through a wire. Take away what holds the store, and the energy comes out. The trigger can be tiny, such as a match, while the store is huge, such as a whole forest. The trigger does not supply the energy. It only lets the energy out.
examples: A match lets out the chemical energy of firewood.
Letting go of a band lets out its stretch.
Pressing a switch closes a circuit and lets out the energy of a cell.
explanations.art: A hand holding a pulled-back catapult beside a closed tap on a tank and a match beside a pile of sticks, each labelled with what holds it.

explanations.concept: Chemical energy: energy stored in how atoms are joined
explanations.definition: Chemical energy is energy stored in the way atoms are joined into molecules. It comes out when the atoms join up in a new way that holds them more tightly.
explanations.description: Food and fuel are made of atoms joined in particular patterns. When your body, or a flame, rearranges them with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, energy comes out as movement and heat. Chemical stores are very big. One medium banana holds about 100 kilocalories, which is about 420 000 joules. To store that much in height, you would have to lift a small apple about 420 kilometres up, if gravity stayed as strong as it is on the ground. A cell or a phone battery is also a chemical store. Its chemicals react slowly, and push electrons round a wire. Fat holds about 9 kilocalories in every gram, and sugar and starch hold about 4.
examples: A banana holds about 420 000 joules.
A kitchen gas cylinder holds chemical energy until the lighter is lit.
A torch cell is a small chemical store.
explanations.art: A banana on one side of a scale and a tiny apple hanging very high above Earth on the other, with a label saying the same energy.

explanations.concept: Refilling a store: charging, eating and pumping
explanations.definition: A store is refilled when energy is put back into it. A rechargeable battery is charged, a body is fed, and a high tank is pumped full.
explanations.description: A charger pushes the chemical change in a rechargeable battery backwards, so the chemicals are ready to react again. A plant fills her own store when sunlight builds sugar from air and water. You fill yours when you eat. Pumped storage fills a store of height. A power station pumps water uphill when electricity is cheap and plentiful, and runs it back down through a turbine when electricity is needed. Such a power station gets back about 70 to 80 of every 100 units it put in. The rest is lost as heat. A store moves energy through time, from when it is plentiful to when it is wanted, even though it gives back a little less than it took.
examples: A phone charges overnight and runs all day.
A parent plant fills each seed with starch before the dry season.
The Kadamparai dam in Tamil Nadu pumps water uphill when power is cheap.
explanations.art: A phone charging beside a plant in sunlight and a lake with a pump pushing water uphill, all with arrows pointing into a store.

explanations.concept: Where every store comes from: nearly all of it traces back to the Sun
explanations.definition: Almost all the stored energy we use began as sunlight. A few stores come from elsewhere: uranium, the tides and the heat inside the Earth.
explanations.description: Follow a dosa back. You eat it, so its energy came from rice. The rice plant built her grain from sunlight. Petrol is the stored sunlight of tiny sea plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. The water in a dam was lifted by the Sun, which evaporated it from the sea, and it fell on the hills as rain. Wind is air moved by the Sun's uneven heating. Some stores are different. Uranium atoms were made in stars that exploded or collided, long before the Sun was born. The tides come from the Moon's pull and the Earth's spinning. The heat deep in the Earth is left over from when it formed, and from slow breakdown of radioactive atoms.
examples: A dosa traces back to sunlight on a rice field.
Petrol traces back to sunlight millions of years ago.
A nuclear power station uses uranium made in dead stars.
explanations.art: The Sun at the top with arrows going down to a rice plant, a rain cloud over a dam and a wind turbine, and a separate arrow to uranium from an exploding star.

explanations.concept: Stores turn into movement and back, but a little always spreads out as heat
explanations.definition: Energy moves between stores and movement, and the total stays the same. Each time, a little of it ends up as spread-out heat and sound that cannot be gathered back.
explanations.description: Drop a ball. The energy of height turns into movement, then into a squash in the ball, then back into movement and height again. But the ball never rises quite as high as it began. Some energy turned into a little sound and a little heat in the ball and the floor. It is not lost from the world. It is spread out so thinly that you cannot use it to lift the ball again. So a ball dropped on its own can never bounce above its starting height. This is why a perpetual motion machine, which is a machine meant to run for ever with no energy put in, always fails. Movement energy also grows faster than speed. A thing moving twice as fast has four times the energy. That is why a cycle going at 20 kilometres an hour needs about four times the distance to stop as one going at 10.
examples: A ball bounces lower each time.
A swing slowly stops unless you keep pumping.
A speeding auto needs a much longer stop than a slow one.
explanations.art: A ball bouncing three times, each bounce lower than the last, with wavy lines of heat and sound near the floor.

explanations.concept: Where is the energy of a lifted ball?
explanations.description: Schools often say that the ball has potential energy. Physicists mostly say that the energy belongs to the ball and the Earth together. If you lifted the ball with no Earth below it, no energy would be stored. The amount also depends on how far the ball can fall. Held over a table, it can give back a little. Held over a floor, the same ball can give back more. So physicists say that only changes in stored energy have meaning, and that where we start counting from is a choice. Some physicists go further and say the energy sits in the field of gravity between the two. In Einstein's theory of gravity, nobody has agreed on where gravity's energy is. This is still discussed.
examples: The same ball over a table and over a floor gives back different amounts.
A stretched band stores its energy in the long chains of molecules in the rubber, which are pulled out of their loose tangle.
A ball lifted in empty space far from any planet would store almost nothing.

perspectives.explanation: The ball has the energy. It is a simple way of speaking, and it gives the right numbers for most problems.
The energy belongs to the ball and the Earth together. Pull them apart and you store energy. It depends on where the ball can fall to.
The energy is in the field of gravity between them. In Einstein's theory, nobody has found a way to say exactly where gravity's energy sits, and this is still discussed.

explanations.art: A ball held above a table and the same ball held in the same place above a floor, with dotted lines showing the two different falls.

explanations.concept: The deepest store: the energy in matter itself
explanations.definition: Matter is itself a store of energy. Einstein's equation E = mc² says that every gram of matter is equal to about 90 trillion joules.
explanations.description: In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy are two forms of one thing. One gram, about the mass of a paper clip, is equal to about 90 trillion joules. That is the energy of about 21 000 tonnes of explosive. Nearly all of it stays locked up. When a Sun-like star joins hydrogen atoms into helium, only about 0.7 percent of the mass turns to energy. Even so, the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of itself into light every second. Fission, where a heavy atom splits, also releases a little of this store. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained fission in 1939 and worked out the energy it releases. Meitner's colleague Otto Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery.
examples: The Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of mass into light each second.
A nuclear power station releases a little of the energy in uranium atoms.
A paper clip, if all its mass could become energy, would equal about 21 000 tonnes of explosive.
explanations.art: A small paper clip beside a huge glowing Sun, joined by a line labelled the same kind of store.

agreed.text: Lifting a thing stores energy in proportion to its weight and its height. Twice the height or twice the weight stores twice the energy.
agreed.evidence: In clay tests since the 1720s and in simple home tests, balls dropped from different heights make dents or bounces that grow in step with the drop height.

agreed.text: For a spring, the pull grows in step with the stretch, so the stored energy grows faster than the stretch. Twice the stretch stores about four times the energy.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hooke published this rule in 1678. Every spring tested since follows it until the spring is overstretched.

agreed.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. It moves between stores and between things, and some of it spreads out as heat.
agreed.evidence: James Joule's experiments in the 1840s showed that a falling weight turning a paddle in water warmed the water by a small and exact amount.

agreed.text: Almost all the energy stored in food, fuel, rain and wind began as sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Plants build sugar from light, coal and oil come from ancient plants and sea life, and the Sun lifts the water and drives the winds.

agreed.text: Fat holds about 9 kilocalories in a gram, while sugar and starch hold about 4. Chemical stores in food are much larger than the stores of height we use at home.
agreed.evidence: Burning food in a sealed container and measuring the heat, a method used since the 1800s, gives these figures.

agreed.text: A ball dropped alone cannot bounce higher than it fell, because every bounce loses a little energy as heat and sound.
agreed.evidence: Every bounce test ever made shows lower bounces. A ball can rise higher only if another store gives it more energy.

challenging.claim: Energy gets used up, and a flat battery has no energy left.
challenging.who: Many people, and many textbooks that talk about using up energy.
challenging.for: A battery goes flat, a ball stops bouncing and a moving cycle slows down.
challenging.against: Measurements find the energy again as heat in the battery, the floor and the air. Nothing disappears, but the spread-out heat is too thin to use.

challenging.claim: A moving ball hits twice as hard if it moves twice as fast.
challenging.who: Descartes, and many followers of Newton in the early 1700s.
challenging.for: It is a simple rule and it seems natural: twice the speed gives twice the force.
challenging.against: Willem 's Gravesande's clay tests in the 1720s showed that twice the speed digs a dent four times as deep. Movement energy grows with the square of the speed.

challenging.claim: The ball holds its own energy, like a number written on it.
challenging.for: It is a short way of speaking, and the sums come out right.
challenging.against: The same ball held in the same place stores more energy over a floor than over a table. The energy depends on the ball and what is below it.

challenging.claim: A ball can bounce higher than the place it was dropped from.
challenging.who: People who have seen two balls dropped together.
challenging.for: When a small ball sits on top of a larger one and both are dropped, the small one can shoot up much higher than the start.
challenging.against: A single ball cannot. With two balls, the extra height comes from energy passed on by the big ball, which almost stops. No energy is made.

challenging.claim: A machine can be built that gives out more energy than it takes in.
challenging.who: Inventors for many centuries, including the Indian mathematician Bhaskara II, who described a wheel of this kind around 1150.
challenging.for: A wheel with weights that swing out looks as if it should always fall on one side.
challenging.against: Nobody has ever built one that works. It would break the rule that energy is never made. Patent offices today refuse such claims.

big_questions.q: A ball held high stores energy. If the Earth vanished, would the ball still hold that energy? What does your answer tell you about where the energy is?
big_questions.hint: In the Table or Floor activity, you held a ball in the same place over a stool and then over the floor. Think about why the bounce was higher over the floor.

big_questions.q: A band pulled back twice as far makes a bar of soap slide more than twice as far. Why might the last centimetre of pull put in more energy than the first?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the band does to your fingers as you stretch it.

big_questions.q: A flat battery and a bouncing ball that has stopped have not lost their energy. It has spread out as heat. If it is still there, why can we not use it?
big_questions.hint: Think about trying to gather the warmth out of a whole room.

big_questions.q: A gram of anything holds as much energy as 21 000 tonnes of explosive, if it could all come out. Where is all that energy hiding?
big_questions.hint: Einstein's equation says mass is a store of energy. Nobody knows all of what that means.

big_questions.q: Coal and oil are sunlight stored over millions of years, and people have used much of it in about two hundred. Is it fair to use a store that took so long to fill?
big_questions.hint: Think about who comes after us, and who has used the most so far.

big_questions.q: A family with a battery or a roof tank can keep going in a power cut, but a family without one cannot. Should energy stores be something everyone can share?
big_questions.hint: Think about who can afford a store, and what a school or a clinic needs.

big_questions.q: Lise Meitner helped explain fission, but the Nobel Prize for it went to Otto Hahn alone. How should we decide who gets the credit for an idea?
big_questions.hint: Think about the people who explained it, the people who found it, and the people who were left out.

big_questions.q: A camel stores fat in her hump, a bird stores fat before a long flight, and a seed stores starch. What does a store let a living being do that she could not do without it?
big_questions.hint: Think about a time when there is no food.

story.title: The Tank on the Rock
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Pumped storage power stations, such as the one at Kadamparai in the hills of Tamil Nadu, pump water uphill when electricity is plentiful and let it run down through turbines when it is needed. Such a station gives back about three-quarters of the energy it took. Tamilselvi's small school version is imagined.
text: In the hills above Valparai, the monsoon rain came sideways, and every evening at six o'clock the electricity went away. It did not come back until after midnight.

Tamilselvi was ten. She lived in the tea estate colony with her mother, who picked tea, and her cousin Karthik, who was thirteen and knew everything. Each evening, they did their homework by one small lamp. It smoked, and it gave a yellow light the size of a plate.

On the roof of the little school stood a panel that turned sunshine into electricity. The estate had paid for it, and it worked best at noon. But at noon the school was nearly empty. The children were at the tea rows, or in lessons that needed no lights. The best electricity of the day was made when nobody wanted it. By six o'clock, when everybody did, the sun was gone.
'What a waste,' said Tamilselvi.
'That is how electricity works,' said Karthik. He snapped his notebook shut, very pleased with himself. 'You cannot keep it. It is like the wind. Use it when it comes, or lose it.'

Tamilselvi did not answer. She was looking out of the window at the big rock behind the school. On top of the rock sat a black water tank, as big as a small room, with a pipe running down to the school. Every noon, the panel's pump filled the tank, so the school had water all night. The water just sat up there, doing nothing.

Or was it doing nothing? She remembered her teacher, Mrs. Rani, lifting a heavy book high above the desk. 'My arm spent energy to lift this,' Mrs. Rani had said. 'Where did that energy go? It did not vanish. It is waiting up here with the book. Let go, and it comes out as a fall.'
Tamilselvi turned round. 'Karthik,' she said slowly, 'the noon sun can lift water up the hill. And water that is up there can fall. And water that falls can turn a wheel.'
Karthik laughed. 'A wheel. And then the wheel makes light? You would need a dynamo.'
'There is one on the old cycle in the shed,' said Tamilselvi.
He stopped laughing.

It took them three Sundays. They cut a plastic drum into cups, and fixed the cups round the rim of an old cycle wheel. They bent the end of the school's water pipe so that the water would strike the cups. They tied the dynamo to the wheel, and a bulb to the dynamo. The first Sunday, nothing happened. The second Sunday, the bulb glowed the colour of weak tea. On the third, Mrs. Rani helped them point the pipe straight at the cups, and the bulb shone a clear white.
Karthik wrote numbers in his notebook. 'It gives back less than the pump took,' he said. 'The pump worked for four hours at noon. The bulb burned for only three. Some of the energy is lost.'
'Yes,' said Tamilselvi. 'It turns into heat in the pump, and the pipe, and the wheel. But the noon sun costs nothing, and nobody was using it. And at six o'clock, everyone wants light.'
On Monday evening, the power cut came at six, as always. The whole hill went dark. Tamilselvi walked to the foot of the rock with a torch, put her hand on the big iron valve, and turned it.
Water ran down the pipe with a roar. The wheel spun. The dynamo began to hum. In the window of the little school, a lamp came on, clear and white, the only light on the whole hill.
Children came out of the colony houses and stood in the rain, looking at it. Karthik stood beside Tamilselvi for a long time without speaking.
'So where is the electricity,' he said at last, 'when the tank is full and the lamp is off?'

Tamilselvi thought about it. 'Up there,' she said, and pointed at the dark tank on the rock. 'In the water, and in all that height between the water and the valley. It is not gone. It is waiting for the valve.'

Later, Mrs. Rani told them that in the hills of Tamil Nadu, a dam at Kadamparai does the very same thing, with a whole lake instead of a drum. 'They pump water up when electricity is plentiful,' she said, 'and let it down when it is needed. It is a battery made of water.'
Tamilselvi nodded. 'Then I did not invent a trick,' she said. 'I only turned a tank on a rock into a lamp that I can switch on at six o'clock.'
On Tuesday, it was Karthik who asked her how a wheel could make light. She told him, and this time he listened.
story.epiphany: Energy does not have to be used when it is made. Lifting water stores the noon sun's energy in height, and a valve lets it out at six o'clock. A store gives back a little less than it was given, but it carries energy from when it is plentiful to when it is wanted.
ask: Why did Tamilselvi lift water at noon and let it down at six o'clock?
What held the energy back in the tank, and what was the trigger that let it out?
The wheel gave back less energy than the pump took. Where did the missing energy go?

games.title: Store and Trigger: a card game
games.players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a card game about stores of energy. Each card shows something that is holding energy. You say what kind of store it is and what lets the energy out.

setup.art: Four labels laid in a row on a table: height, stretch or squash, chemical, and not a store, with a pile of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four labels. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading the front of a card showing a coconut high on a palm, then pointing to the height label.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Say which store it is and what the trigger is.

setup.art: The card turned over, showing the answer, with two score tokens beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check. Score a point for each right answer.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: something that holds energy on the front, and the store and trigger on the back

items.b: Chemical store. The trigger is opening the regulator and lighting a flame. The energy comes out as heat and light.

items.b: Chemical store, in the battery. The trigger is switching the phone on. The energy comes out as light, sound and a little heat.
