items.f: A child at the top of a slide, holding the rails.
items.b: Height store. The trigger is letting go. The energy comes out as sliding and speed.

items.f: A ballpoint pen with its spring squashed and the tip out.
items.b: Squash store, in a spring. The trigger is pressing the click button again. The energy comes out as the tip popping back in.

items.f: A door closer with its arm pulled open.
items.b: Stretch or squash store, in a spring. The trigger is letting go of the door. The energy comes out as the door swinging shut.

items.f: A heap of firewood in a yard.
items.b: Chemical store. The trigger is a lit match or any strong heat. The energy comes out as heat and light.

items.f: A plate of rice and sambar in front of you.
items.b: Chemical store, in the food. The trigger is eating and digesting it. The energy comes out as warmth and movement in your body.

items.f: A bicycle tyre pumped hard, with the valve closed.
items.b: Squash store, in compressed air. The trigger is opening the valve. The energy comes out as a rush of air.

items.f: A balloon blown up and held shut at the neck.
items.b: Squash and stretch store, in squashed air and stretched rubber. The trigger is letting go of the neck. The energy comes out as the air rushing out and the balloon darting off.

items.f: A diver stands on the end of a bent diving board.
items.b: Bend store. The trigger is the diver jumping, which lets the board spring back. The energy comes out as a push upward.

items.f: A wound-up toy car, held still in your hand.
items.b: Twist store, in a spring. The trigger is letting go of the car. The energy comes out as the car running.

items.f: A boulder sits on a hilltop, held by a little soil.
items.b: Height store. The trigger is heavy rain washing the soil away, or a push. The energy comes out as a rolling fall.

items.f: A diya full of oil that is not yet lit.
items.b: Chemical store. The trigger is the flame of a match. The energy comes out as light and heat.

items.f: A dam full of water, with its gates shut.
items.b: Height store. The trigger is opening the gates. The energy comes out as rushing water that can turn a turbine.

items.f: The head of an unlit matchstick.
items.b: Chemical store. The trigger is rubbing it on the box, which makes heat. The energy comes out as flame.

items.f: A camel's hump.
items.b: Chemical store, in fat. The trigger is the body needing energy when food and water are short. The energy comes out as fuel for the camel's body.

items.f: A catapult (a Y-shaped slingshot) pulled back and held.
items.b: Stretch store. The trigger is letting go. The energy comes out as the movement of the stone.

items.f: A book lying flat on the floor.
items.b: Not a store, compared with this floor, because the book cannot fall any further. It would store energy if there were a hole below it.

items.f: A football rolling across a field.
items.b: Not a store. It holds movement energy, which is energy that is already out.

items.f: A rubber band lying loose on a table.
items.b: Not a store, because it is not stretched. Stretch it and it becomes one.

items.f: A hot cup of chai on a table.
items.b: Not a store you can release as a push. The heat is spread among the chai's tiny particles, and it slowly spreads out into the air.

rules: Lay the 4 labels in a row. Shuffle the 24 cards and make a pile with the writing side up.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front. Say which label it goes under, and what the trigger is.
Turn the card over and check the back. Score 1 point if the store is right, and 1 more if the trigger is right.
Some cards are not stores at all. If you say so, and you are right, score 2 points.
If you are wrong, read the back out loud and put the card at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is done, add up the points. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to score 36 or more.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the labels and the cards. 2. Lay the 4 labels in a row. 3. Shuffle the cards and make a pile.
flow.say: Each card shows something that may hold energy. You say what kind of store it is, and what lets the energy out. Lay out the four labels first.
flow.kid: Each card shows a thing that may hold energy. Say what store it is. Say what lets the energy out.
flow.context: This is the first step of Store and Trigger. You set up the game.
flow.parent: No printer or scissors? Copy each front on a slip of paper, or read the fronts from the screen while someone else holds the backs. With 2 to 4 players, take turns, and the others may help with a hint. This game is cards only: never light a match, diya or stove for it. A grown-up should do any cutting.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. For each, read the front, say the store and the trigger, and then check the back.
flow.say: Take a card. Read the front. Which label does it go under? What is the trigger? Then turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Take a card. Pick a label. Say the trigger. Turn it over.

ask.q: What is holding the energy back on this card?
good: A hand.
A closed tap.
A spring that is held.
The chemicals are kept apart.

flow.parent: Let your child answer before they turn the card. If they pick the wrong store, read the back together and move on. It is a game, not a test.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards.

flow.do: Find the four trick cards in the pile: the book, the football, the loose band and the chai. Play them now. Let your child spot why each is not a store.
flow.say: Some cards are tricks. A book on the floor cannot fall any further. A rolling football has energy that is already out. Can you spot why each is not a store?
flow.kid: Some cards are tricks. Is the thing a store, or not? Why?
flow.parent: The book card matters most. A book on a floor stores nothing compared with that floor, but over a hole it would. This is the same idea as the Table or Floor activity.
flow.context: In this step, you meet the trick cards that are not stores.

flow.do: Finish the pile, add up the points, and ask: which kind of store did you find hardest to spot?
flow.say: Add up your points. Which kind of store was hardest to spot? Which trigger surprised you?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which store was hardest to spot?
flow.context: This is the last step of Store and Trigger. You count points and talk.

games.title: Back to the Sun: trace the energy home
games.players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a card game about where energy comes from. Each card shows something that uses energy. You trace its energy back, step by step, to where it began.

setup.art: A pile of cards with the Sun drawn at the top of a sheet of paper and a row of empty boxes below it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Draw the Sun on a sheet of paper.

setup.art: A child looking at the front of a card showing a lit diya, and counting off links on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Say the chain back to the Sun, link by link.

setup.art: The card turned over with the chain written on the back, and a child pointing to each link she got right.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check the chain. Score a point for each link.

printables.title: 16 two-sided cards: something that uses energy on the front, and its chain back to the source on the back

items.f: A hot idli on your plate.
items.b: Sunlight, then rice and dal plants that build their grain from light, then the grain, then the idli, then you.

items.f: An LED bulb lit by a coal power station.
items.b: Sunlight long ago, then ancient plants, then coal, then heat and steam, then a turbine, then electricity, then the bulb.

items.f: An auto-rickshaw running on petrol.
items.b: Sunlight long ago, then tiny sea plants and animals, then oil, then petrol, then the engine.

items.f: Water falling through a hydro power station, such as the one at Idukki in Kerala.
items.b: The Sun heats the sea, then the water rises and falls as rain on the hills, then it is held high in the dam, then it falls through the turbine.

items.f: A wind turbine turning near Muppandal in Tamil Nadu.
items.b: The Sun heats land and sea unevenly, then the air moves as wind, then the wind turns the blades.

items.f: A lamp lit by a rooftop solar panel.
items.b: Sunlight, then the panel, then electricity, then the lamp. This is the shortest chain.

items.f: A lit diya of ghee.
items.b: Sunlight, then grass, then a cow, then milk, then butter, then ghee, then the flame.

items.f: You throw a cricket ball.
items.b: Sunlight, then plants, then your food, then your muscles, then the throw.

items.f: Firewood burning in a chulha.
items.b: Sunlight, then a tree that builds wood, then the dry wood, then the fire.

items.f: Biogas burning in a village kitchen.
items.b: Sunlight, then plants, then cattle eating them, then dung, then microbes that make gas, then the flame.

items.f: A migrating bar-headed goose flying over the Himalayas.
items.b: Sunlight, then plants, then seeds and grass, then the goose's fat, then her flight.

items.f: A coconut hanging high on a palm.
items.b: Sunlight, then the palm, which builds her trunk and lifts her fruit high with the light she collects.

items.f: A nuclear power station, such as the one at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu.
items.b: Not the Sun. Uranium atoms were made in exploding and colliding stars, long before the Sun was born. Score 3 for spotting this.

items.f: The tide coming in at a beach.
items.b: Not the Sun alone. The tides come mostly from the Moon's pull and the Earth's spinning, and the Sun adds a little. Score 3 for spotting this.

items.f: A hot spring at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh.
items.b: Not the Sun. The heat comes from inside the Earth, left over from when the Earth formed, and from the slow breakdown of radioactive atoms. Score 3 for spotting this.

items.f: A phone charging from the mains.
items.b: It depends on the power station. In India most mains electricity comes from coal, which is ancient sunlight. Trace as far as you can.

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and make a pile with the writing side up.
On your turn, take a card and read the front. You have 30 seconds to say the chain from where it began to the thing on the card.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point for each link you got right.
Some cards do not begin with the Sun. If you spot that, score 3 points.
Put the card at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is done, add up the points. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your own score the next day.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Shuffle them into a pile. 3. Agree on 30 seconds for each card.
flow.say: Each card shows something that uses energy. You trace its energy back to where it began. You have thirty seconds for each card.
flow.kid: Each card uses energy. Trace it back to where it began. You have thirty seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of Back to the Sun. You set up the game.
flow.parent: You need something that shows 30 seconds, such as a phone timer or counting aloud. With 2 to 4 players, take turns, and the others may help with a missing link for half a point. A grown-up should do any cutting.

flow.do: Play eight cards. For each, say the chain out loud before you check the back.
flow.say: Take a card. Say the chain out loud, from where the energy began to the thing on the card. Then check the back.
flow.kid: Take a card. Say the chain. Then check the back.

ask.q: Where was the energy before it reached this thing?
good: It was sunlight.
It was stored in a plant.
It was held in water high up.

flow.parent: Most chains start with the Sun. A chain with fewer links is not worse. The aim is to find where the energy began.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards.

flow.do: Finish the pile. Ask which cards did not begin with the Sun, and why.
flow.say: Which cards did not begin with the Sun? Where did their energy come from?
flow.kid: Which cards did not begin with the Sun? Why?
flow.parent: The three exceptions are uranium from stars, the tides from the Moon, and the heat from inside the Earth. Even uranium's energy was made in stars, so every store has a beginning.
flow.context: This is the last step of Back to the Sun. You look at the exceptions.

experiments.title: The Soap Slider: does twice the pull-back give twice the slide?
experiments.question: A pulled-back rubber band pushes a bar of soap along the floor. If you pull the soap back twice as far, does it slide twice as far, or more, or less?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How far will the soap slide after a 2 centimetre pull-back, and after a 4 centimetre pull-back? Will twice the pull-back give twice the slide? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same band, the same soap, the same pencils and the same floor are used every time. The pencils are always 10 centimetres apart. The soap always starts straight behind the band, and you always let go of it without flicking. Only the pull-back changes, so any change in the slide comes from the pull-back. Each pull-back is tried three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 2 pencils (a new pencil is not needed; any stub with a point will do)
2 lumps of clay or atta dough, each about the size of a lemon, and a few strips of masking tape to stick them to the floor
1 rubber band that is just snug when it goes round both pencils 10 centimetres apart
a bar of soap of about 75 to 100 grams, with flat sides
a 30 centimetre ruler, and a tailor's tape or a long tape measure
a smooth floor of tiles or cement with 2 metres clear in front of the pencils
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: A rubber band can snap, so stand to the side of the band's line and never pull the soap back more than 6 centimetres. Push each pencil with the pointed end deep into the clay and the flat end up, so nobody can fall on a point. Tape the clay lumps to the floor. Keep your face away from the band. A grown-up should be near, because pencils are sharp.
experiments.record: Write each slide in the table. Circle the middle one of the three for each pull-back. Then draw a bar for each pull-back, using the middle slide.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you pull a rubber band back by different amounts and measure how far it pushes a bar of soap. You find out how much more energy a longer pull-back stores.

setup.art: Two pencils standing in lumps of clay taped to a tiled floor, 10 centimetres apart, with a rubber band round both of them low down, about 2 centimetres above the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Stand two pencils in clay, 10 centimetres apart, and tape the clay to the floor. Put the band round both, low down.

setup.art: A ruler laid on the floor behind the band and a tape laid in front of it, both with their zero at the band, and a bar of soap touching the band.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a ruler behind the band and a tape in front. Put the soap against the band.

setup.art: A child's hand sliding the soap straight back along the ruler until its front edge is at the 2 centimetre mark, with the band bent into a V.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the soap straight back to 2 centimetres. The band bends into a V.

setup.art: The soap sliding away between the pencils and stopping on the tape, with a finger pointing at the front edge of the soap.
setup.caption: 4. Let go. Read where the front of the soap stops on the tape.

flow.do: Show your child the soap, the band and the pencils. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will pull a rubber band back and let go. It will push a bar of soap along the floor. How far will the soap slide after a 2 centimetre pull-back? And after a 4 centimetre pull-back, which is twice as far? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A band will push a bar of soap along the floor. Pull the soap back 2 centimetres, then 4. How far will it slide each time? Why do you think so?

ask.q: If we pull back twice as far, will the soap slide twice as far, or more, or less? Why?
good: Twice as far, because the pull is twice as long.
More, because the band is stretched more.
Less, because the band gets tired.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guess and the reason at the top of the table. Use a smooth tile or cement floor, because a carpet will not work. With 2 to 4 children, give each child a job: one pulls and lets go, one reads the tape and calls the number, one writes. Swap jobs after each pull-back size. Every child writes their own guess first. With one child, you read the tape and write while your child pulls and lets go.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Soap Slider. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Push the pointed end of each pencil into a lump of clay and tape the clay to the floor. 2. Stand the pencils exactly 10 centimetres apart. 3. Loop the band round both pencils, low down, about 2 centimetres above the floor, so it is straight and just snug. 4. Lay the ruler behind the band and the tape in front, with their zeros at the band.
flow.say: Stand the two pencils exactly 10 centimetres apart. Put the band round both. It should be straight, and only just snug. Lay the ruler behind the band, and the tape in front. Both start at zero on the band.
flow.kid: Stand two pencils in clay, 10 centimetres apart. Put the band round them. Lay the ruler behind it and the tape in front.
flow.parent: Check the band. If it is loose and floppy, use a smaller band. If it is already very tight, move the pencils a little closer. If the pencils tip over or lean towards you, press more clay round their feet and add tape. Keep the band low, because a band high up tips the pencils. Soap with a flat side works best, because a round soap can roll.

check.q: Why must the pencils always be exactly 10 centimetres apart?
options: So the band is the same every test, and only the pull-back changes
So the soap looks neat
So the pencils do not touch
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the pencils moved, the band would be tighter or looser, and you would not know whether the pull-back or the band made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you build the launcher that you will use for every test.

flow.do: 1. Put the soap against the band, in the middle between the pencils. 2. Slide it straight back until its front edge is at 2 centimetres on the ruler. 3. Let go. Do not flick it. 4. Read where the front edge stops on the tape, and write the number. 5. Do this three times.
flow.say: Put the soap against the band. Slide it back until its front edge is at 2 centimetres. Let go, without flicking. Read where the front edge stops. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Pull the soap back 2 centimetres. Let go. Read where it stops. Do it three times.

ask.q: What does the band do to the soap when you let go?
good: It pushes it forward.
It springs back and shoves the soap.
It gives the soap a kick.

flow.parent: The soap leaves the band when the band is straight again at the pencils. If the soap barely moves, write the small number or 0. That is a real result. If the soap skids sideways, start again and slide it straight back. Put the soap in the same spot each time. If even the 6 centimetre pull-back moves the soap less than about 10 centimetres, the band is too weak: use a thicker band, or two bands side by side, or move the pencils 2 centimetres closer. If the soap flies far even at 2 centimetres, use a thinner band.
flow.context: In this step, you try the smallest pull-back and measure how far the soap slides.

flow.do: 1. Slide the soap back until its front edge is at 4 centimetres on the ruler. 2. Let go. 3. Read where the front edge stops on the tape, and write the number. 4. Do this three times.
flow.say: Now pull the soap back to 4 centimetres. That is twice as far as before. Let go, and read where it stops. Do it three times. Is the slide twice as far?
flow.kid: Now pull the soap back 4 centimetres, twice as far. Let go. Read where it stops. Do it three times.

ask.q: How does this slide compare with the 2 centimetre slide?
good: It is much longer.
It is more than twice as far.
It is about four times as far.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Let your child compare the numbers. Expect the slide to be more than twice the first one, often 3 to 10 times. Yours may differ.
flow.context: In this step, you double the pull-back and measure the slide again.

flow.do: 1. Slide the soap back until its front edge is at 6 centimetres on the ruler. 2. Stand to the side. 3. Let go, read where it stops, and write the number. 4. Do this three times.
flow.say: Last, pull the soap back to 6 centimetres. Stand to one side. Let go, and read where it stops. Do it three times. Do not go further than 6.
flow.kid: Pull the soap back 6 centimetres. Stand to the side. Let go. Read where it stops. Do it three times.
flow.parent: If the soap flies off the end of the tape, write 'more than' and the length of the tape. If the band feels very tight or thin, stop and use a thicker band. Do not pull back more than 6 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step, you try the longest pull-back. The band is stretched the most, so stand to the side.

flow.do: 1. In each row of the table, circle the middle of the three slides. 2. Draw a bar for each pull-back. 3. Divide the 4 centimetre slide by the 2 centimetre slide. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? How many times as far did the soap slide when we doubled the pull-back?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each pull-back. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After your child has said what they saw, you can explain. The soap slides until friction with the floor uses up all the energy the band gave it. So the slide shows how much energy the band passed on. Bands differ a lot, so your numbers may be small or large. Twice the pull-back usually gives much more than twice the slide, often 3 to 10 times, but with a very small first slide the ratio is not reliable. If the 2 centimetre slide is under 2 centimetres, compare the 6 centimetre slide with the 4 centimetre slide instead. Two things add up. The band pulls harder the more it is stretched. And the soap pulls the band into a V shape, which stretches it more and more for each extra centimetre. If your numbers differ, say so. Real rubber is not a perfect spring.
flow.think: Why did a pull-back twice as long make the soap slide more than twice as far?

check.q: The 2 centimetre pull-back gave a slide of 12 centimetres. The 4 centimetre pull-back gave 48 centimetres. What does this show?
options: Doubling the pull-back stored about four times the energy
Doubling the pull-back stored twice the energy
The band did not matter, only the soap
check.why: 48 divided by 12 is 4. The soap slides until floor friction has used up its energy, so a slide 4 times as long means about 4 times the energy. If you picked twice, you assumed the energy grows in step with the pull-back. The Soap Slider test shows that it grows faster.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Soap Slider. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Bounce Ratio: how high does a ball come back from different heights?
experiments.question: A ball dropped from a height bounces back up. If you drop it from twice the height, does it bounce twice as high, or more, or less?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the ball come back up to where it was dropped from? Will a drop from twice the height give a bounce twice as high? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same ball, the same floor and the same helper are used for every drop. You always let the ball go without pushing it down, with the top of the ball at the mark. The helper always reads the top of the ball at its highest point from the same eye level. Only the drop height changes. Each height is tried three times, because one try can be a fluke. A ball of dough is the control: it shows what happens with no spring.

materials.item: a ball that bounces well, such as a cricket tennis ball or a rubber ball (a ball that is flat or soft will bounce badly)
a ball of dough or clay about the same size as the ball
a tailor's tape or a metre stick, stuck upright on a wall with zero at the floor
masking tape, for flags at 30, 60 and 90 centimetres
a hard floor beside the wall, such as tiles or cement
a helper to watch the bounce, and a phone to film it if you have one (with one child, the phone is the helper)
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the floor clear so nobody steps on the ball. Do the test away from fans, windows and shelves of glass.
experiments.record: Write each bounce in the table. Circle the middle one of three for each drop height. Then divide the bounce by the drop and write the answer as a fraction or a decimal.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you drop a ball from three heights and measure how high it bounces. You find out how much of the energy comes back.

setup.art: A tape measure stuck upright on a wall with zero at the floor, and three small tape flags at 30, 60 and 90 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Stick the tape on the wall with zero at the floor. Mark 30, 60 and 90 centimetres.

setup.art: A child holding a ball with its top at the 30 centimetre flag, while a helper crouches at eye level beside the tape.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ball with its top at the mark. The helper crouches beside the tape.

setup.art: A ball bouncing up beside the tape, with the helper's finger pointing to the highest point of the top of the ball.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. The helper reads the highest point of the top of the ball.

setup.art: A ball of dough lying flat on the floor after being dropped, next to a bouncing ball.
setup.caption: 4. Drop the dough ball too. It does not bounce.

flow.do: Show your child the ball and the dough ball. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will drop this ball from 30, 60 and 90 centimetres. Will it come back up to where we dropped it from? If we drop it from twice as high, will it bounce twice as high? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop a ball from 30, 60 and 90 centimetres. Will it bounce back up to the start? Why do you think so?

ask.q: When the ball comes back up, will it reach the place it was dropped from? Why?
good: Yes, because the ball springs back.
No, because some energy is lost.
A bit lower, because the floor takes some of the energy.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guess and reason at the top of the table. Most people think the ball comes back all the way, or they have not thought about it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bounce Ratio. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stick the tape upright on the wall, with zero at the floor. 2. Put a flag of masking tape at 30, 60 and 90 centimetres. 3. Practise one drop at 30. The helper crouches so their eyes are level with the flag.
flow.say: Stick the tape on the wall. Zero is at the floor. Put a flag at 30, 60 and 90. Your helper crouches next to the tape. Their eyes should be level with the top of the bounce.
flow.kid: Stick the tape on the wall. Put flags at 30, 60 and 90. The helper crouches beside it.
flow.parent: A bounce is quick. If you have a phone, film each drop in slow motion with the tape in view, then pause at the top of the bounce. Without a phone, practise a few drops so the helper learns where to look. With 2 to 4 children, give jobs: one drops, one reads the bounce at eye level, one films, one writes. Swap after each height, and let a second reader check. With one child, stand the phone on a pile of books, film each drop, and read the bounce when you play it back. Two readers can differ by a few centimetres; that is why we take the middle of three.

check.q: Why does the helper always crouch at the same eye level?
options: So the height is read from the same angle every time
So the ball bounces higher
So the helper is not hit by the ball
check.why: Looking from above or below makes the top of the ball seem to be at a different mark. Reading from the same eye level keeps the measuring fair.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the measuring wall for the Bounce Ratio.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball with its top at the 30 centimetre flag. 2. Let go, without pushing it. 3. The helper reads the highest point of the top of the ball. 4. Write it down. 5. Do this three times.
flow.say: Hold the ball with its top at 30. Let go, and do not push. Your helper reads how high the top of the ball goes. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Hold the ball at 30. Let go. The helper reads the top of the bounce. Do it three times.

ask.q: How high did the ball come back compared with where it started?
good: Lower than the start.
About two thirds of the way.
Not all the way back.

flow.parent: For 30 centimetres, a cricket tennis ball often bounces about 15 to 22 centimetres, but balls differ, so yours may be higher or lower. If the readings differ by more than 4 centimetres, try again. If the ball bounces hardly at all, it is too soft or the floor is too soft; try a different ball or a tile.
flow.context: In this step, you drop the ball from the lowest mark.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball with its top at the 60 centimetre flag. 2. Let go. 3. The helper reads the top of the bounce. 4. Write it down. 5. Do this three times.
flow.say: Now drop the ball from 60. That is twice as high. Let go, and your helper reads the top of the bounce. Do it three times. Is it twice as high as before?
flow.kid: Now drop the ball from 60, twice as high. The helper reads the bounce. Do it three times.

ask.q: The drop was twice as high. How does the bounce compare with the 30 centimetre bounce?
good: About twice as high.
Higher, but still below the start.
A bit less than twice.

flow.parent: For 60 centimetres, about 30 to 44 centimetres is common. Do not explain yet. Let your child compare the numbers.
flow.context: In this step, you double the drop height and measure the bounce again.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball with its top at the 90 centimetre flag. 2. Let go. 3. The helper reads the top of the bounce. 4. Write it down. 5. Do this three times.
flow.say: Last, drop the ball from 90. That is three times as high as the first drop. The helper reads the top of the bounce. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Last, drop the ball from 90. The helper reads the bounce. Do it three times.
flow.parent: For 90 centimetres, about 45 to 65 centimetres is common. You can try a drop from 120 centimetres if the tape is long enough.
flow.context: In this step, you try the highest drop.

flow.do: 1. Hold the dough ball with its top at the 90 centimetre flag. 2. Let go. 3. Write how high it bounces.
flow.say: Now drop the ball of dough from 90. How high does it bounce? What do you think the dough ball is missing?
flow.kid: Drop the dough ball from 90. How high does it bounce? What is it missing?

ask.q: What does the dough ball not have that the other ball has?
good: It does not spring back.
It does not store the squash.
It stays squashed.

flow.parent: The dough ball lands with a thud and stays squashed. Its energy goes into changing its shape for good and into a little heat. It stores almost none of the squash to give back.
flow.context: In this step, you drop a ball that has no spring. It shows what happens without a store of squash.

flow.do: 1. Circle the middle of the three bounces for each height. 2. Divide each middle bounce by its drop height. 3. Draw a bar for each drop height. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? What fraction of the drop height came back each time?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each drop. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After your child has said what they saw, you can explain. The energy of height turns into movement, then into a squash in the ball, then into movement and height again. Each time, a little turns into heat and sound in the ball and the floor. Many balls return about half to two thirds of the height, and the fraction stays about the same at every drop height. Doubling the drop height doubles the energy stored in height, so the bounce also doubles. If your numbers differ, say so.
flow.think: Why does a ball never bounce back as high as it was dropped from?

check.q: A ball dropped from 40 centimetres bounces to 25. Dropped from 80 centimetres, about how high will it bounce?
options: About 50 centimetres
About 25 centimetres
About 80 centimetres
check.why: The ball returns about the same fraction of its drop height every time. 25 out of 40 is a little more than half. Twice the drop height gives about twice the bounce, so about 50. If you chose 25, you thought the drop height did not matter. If you chose 80, you thought the ball returns all its energy.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bounce Ratio. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

activities.title: Hanging Water: how hard does a band pull back?

materials.item: a thick rubber band
a small empty plastic bottle of 500 millilitres, with a string tied round its neck in a loop
a hook for the band, such as a door handle, a cupboard knob or a pencil resting across two chair backs
a measuring jug marked in millilitres, and water (no jug? use a cough-syrup dose cup or a small glass, and count 'cups' instead of millilitres, with every cup filled to the same line)
a ruler or a paper strip taped upright beside the band
a towel for spills, and paper and a pencil
a tray or a bucket under the bottle, to catch spills

activities.safety: Keep your face away from the band while it holds the bottle. Stop adding water at 400 millilitres, because a band can snap if it is overloaded. Hang it where nobody walks, with a tray under it. Hold the bottle with one hand while you hook it on, and let go slowly.

schedule.what: Guess. Hang the bottle from the band. Add 100 millilitres of water at a time and measure the stretch. Draw a graph and say what you found.

activities.record: A table with the water added in millilitres and the stretch of the band in centimetres. Then a line graph of stretch against water.
activities.context: In this activity, you hang more and more water from a rubber band and measure how far it stretches. You find out how hard a band pulls back, which tells you why a longer pull stores so much more energy.

setup.art: A rubber band hanging from a door handle with a plastic bottle hanging from it by a string loop, and a paper ruler taped beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the empty bottle from the band. Mark where the bottle's string hangs. This is zero.

setup.art: A measuring jug pouring 100 millilitres of water into the hanging bottle while a child holds a hand under it.
setup.caption: 2. Pour in 100 millilitres of water. Wait, then mark and measure the stretch.

setup.art: A table of water and stretch numbers next to a straight line graph drawn on squared paper.
setup.caption: 3. Add 100 millilitres more each time. Write the stretch. Draw the graph.

flow.do: Show your child the band and the bottle. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will hang a bottle from a band and add water, 100 millilitres at a time. The band will stretch. Each time we add the same water, will it stretch the same amount again? Or more, or less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hang a bottle from a band. Add water 100 millilitres at a time. Will the band stretch the same each time? Why?

ask.q: Will every 100 millilitres stretch the band by the same amount? Why?
good: Yes, because the weight is the same.
No, the band gets harder to stretch.
No, it stretches more each time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A guess with a reason is a good start. Water is a good weight, because 100 millilitres weighs about 100 grams. With 2 to 4 children, one pours, one marks, one measures and one writes; swap after each step. With one child, you pour and your child marks and measures.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hanging Water. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Hang the band from a door handle. 2. Hook the string loop of the empty bottle on the band. 3. Tape the ruler upright beside the band. 4. Mark on the ruler where the string hangs. That mark is zero.
flow.say: Hang the band from a door handle. Hook the empty bottle on the band. Tape a ruler beside it. Mark where the string hangs. That is zero stretch.
flow.kid: Hang the band from a door handle. Hook on the empty bottle. Tape a ruler beside it. Mark where the string hangs. That is zero.
flow.parent: A band hung from a door handle works well. The ruler must not touch the string. If the bottle swings, stop it before you read.

check.q: Why do we mark zero with the empty bottle hanging, and not with nothing hanging?
options: The empty bottle already pulls on the band, so the stretch is counted from there
The bottle is heavy
The band is easier to see with a bottle
check.why: The bottle itself has some weight. We want to know how much each 100 millilitres of water adds, so we count from the empty bottle.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the hanging band and mark the starting point.

flow.do: 1. Pour in 100 millilitres of water, slowly. 2. Wait 10 seconds. 3. Mark where the string hangs and measure from zero. 4. Write the stretch. 5. Add 100 millilitres more and repeat, up to 400 millilitres.
flow.say: Pour in 100 millilitres, slowly. Wait ten seconds. Mark where the string hangs. Measure from zero. Do the same with 200, 300 and 400 millilitres.
flow.kid: Add 100 millilitres of water. Wait ten seconds. Mark where the string hangs and measure from zero. Do the same at 200, 300 and 400.

ask.q: Does each 100 millilitres stretch the band by the same amount?
good: About the same each time.
A bit less each time.
It stretches in even steps.

flow.parent: Rubber slowly creeps, so wait before you read. The numbers are only about right: a thin band might stretch about 1 centimetre for each 100 millilitres, and a thick one about half a centimetre. The steps are usually about equal. The first step is often a little different from the rest, and the last steps are often slightly smaller. Stop at 400 millilitres. If the band stretches less than 3 millimetres per step, it is too stiff to read, so use a thinner band or two thin bands together.
flow.context: In this step, you add the same weight again and again and measure the stretch each time.

flow.do: 1. Draw a graph with water on the bottom and stretch up the side. 2. Mark each pair of numbers and join the dots with a ruler. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Where would the line be for 200 millilitres more?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After your child has said what they saw, you can explain. A straight line means that the stretch grows in step with the weight, so the band pulls back twice as hard when it is stretched twice as far. Now think about storing energy. To stretch the band twice as far, you pull twice as hard at the end, and you pull through twice the distance. Twice as hard over twice as far is 2 times 2, which is 4. That is why twice the pull-back stores about four times the energy.
flow.think: If twice the weight gives about twice the stretch, how hard must you pull to hold a band stretched twice as far?

check.q: A band stretches 2 centimetres with 200 millilitres of water. About how much would it stretch with 400 millilitres?
options: About 4 centimetres
About 2 centimetres
About 8 centimetres
check.why: A straight line means twice the weight gives about twice the stretch. If you chose 8, you doubled it twice. If you chose 2, you thought extra weight does not matter.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hanging Water. You draw the graph and explain what you found.

activities.title: Table or Floor: the same ball in the same place

materials.item: the ball from the Bounce Ratio test
a low, hard stool or small table about 40 to 50 centimetres high (wood or steel; a soft plastic top takes energy and spoils the test)
a tailor's tape stuck upright on a wall with zero at the floor, and a flag of masking tape
a 30 centimetre ruler
a helper to watch the bounce

schedule.what: Guess. Drop the ball onto the stool. Take the stool away and drop it from the same place to the floor. Compare the two bounces.

activities.record: Write the bounce height above the stool and the bounce height above the floor. Say how many times higher the second one is.
activities.context: In this activity, you hold a ball in exactly the same place twice. The first time there is a stool below it. The second time the stool is gone. You find out whether the ball stores the same energy both times.

setup.art: A stool standing next to a wall beside a tape, with a flag on the wall 30 centimetres above the stool top.
setup.caption: 1. Put a flag on the wall 30 centimetres above the top of the stool.

setup.art: A child dropping a ball from the flag onto the stool top while a helper holds a ruler upright on the stool.
setup.caption: 2. Drop the ball onto the stool. Read how high it bounces above the stool.

setup.art: The same child dropping the ball from the same flag, with the stool moved away, and the ball falling all the way to the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Take the stool away. Drop from the same flag. Read the bounce above the floor.

flow.do: Show your child the stool and the ball. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will hold the ball in one place, and drop it onto the stool. Then we take the stool away and drop it from the same place. Will the bounces be the same height? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop the ball onto a stool. Take the stool away. Drop the ball from the same spot. Will the bounce be the same? Why?

ask.q: The ball is held in exactly the same place. Will it bounce the same height both times? Why?
good: Yes, because it is the same ball.
No, it falls further the second time.
Higher the second time, because it drops from higher.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The key point is that your child's hand and the ball do not move. Only the stool does.
flow.context: This is the first step of Table or Floor. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stand the stool by the wall. 2. Put a flag on the wall 30 centimetres above the top of the stool. 3. Hold the ball with its top at the flag. 4. Let go. 5. The helper holds the ruler upright on the stool and reads the top of the bounce. Do it three times.
flow.say: Put a flag on the wall, 30 centimetres above the stool top. Hold the ball with its top at the flag. Let go. Your helper reads the bounce above the stool. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Put a flag 30 centimetres above the stool. Drop the ball from the flag. The helper reads the bounce. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Expect a bounce of about 15 to 22 centimetres above the stool top. The stool top can be a different hardness from the floor, so the bounce may differ a little. We are looking for a big change, not a small one. With 2 to 4 children, one drops, one reads the bounce, one writes; swap each round. With one child, the parent reads the bounce.
flow.context: In this step, you drop the ball onto the stool and measure the bounce.

flow.do: 1. Move the stool well away. Do not move the flag. 2. Hold the ball with its top at the same flag. 3. Let go, and it falls to the floor. 4. The helper reads the top of the bounce on the tape, with zero at the floor. Do it three times.
flow.say: Now move the stool away. Leave the flag where it is. Hold the ball in exactly the same place. Let go. Your helper reads the bounce above the floor.
flow.kid: Move the stool away. Keep the flag. Drop the ball from the same spot. The helper reads the bounce.

ask.q: The ball started in exactly the same place. Why is the bounce different?
good: It fell further.
It had a longer way to fall.
It had more energy to give back.

flow.parent: The bounce above the floor should be roughly 2 to 3 times the bounce above the stool. Do not explain yet. Let your child tell you why.
flow.context: In this step, you drop the same ball from the same place, with nothing below it until the floor.

flow.do: Compare the two bounces. Ask: the ball was held in the same place, so why did it give back different amounts?
flow.say: Tell me what you saw. The ball was in exactly the same place both times. Why did it give back more the second time?
flow.kid: Same ball, same place. Why was the second bounce higher?
flow.parent: After your child has said what they saw, you can explain. The energy a ball can give back depends on how far it can fall. With the stool gone, the same ball can fall further, so it can give back more. So the energy is not only in the ball. It depends on the ball and on what is below it.
flow.think: Does a ball in your hand hold one fixed amount of energy?
flow.context: This is the last step of Table or Floor. You say what you found.

activities.safety: Keep the stool steady and by the wall. Nobody should stand on it. Do not play near glass or fans.

activities.title: The Syringe Spring: air that pushes back

materials.item: a 10 millilitre medicine syringe with no needle (the dose syringe that comes with children's medicine works), or a bicycle pump
a small lump of clay to plug the nozzle
a cup of water and a tray or sink, for the last step

activities.safety: Use a syringe with no needle, and keep it out of your mouth. The syringe has small parts, so it is not for children under five. The clay plug can pop out when the air is squashed hard, so never push past 4 millilitres and do not point it at anyone's face. Never point a pump at anyone's face. Do the water step over a tray or sink.

schedule.what: Guess. Plug the syringe and push the plunger. Feel the air push back. Let go and watch. Then try the same with water and compare.

activities.record: Draw the syringe with the plunger pulled back and then pushed in. Draw arrows for the push of the air.
activities.context: In this activity, you squash a small amount of air and feel it push back. You find out that air is a store of energy, like a spring.

setup.art: A medicine syringe with its plunger pulled out to the 10 millilitre mark and the nozzle pressed into a lump of clay.
setup.caption: 1. Pull the plunger to 10 millilitres. Press the nozzle into the clay to block it.

setup.art: A thumb pushing the plunger in to the 5 millilitre mark, with small arrows inside the barrel pushing back.
setup.caption: 2. Push the plunger in. Feel the air push back.

setup.art: The plunger springing back to near the 10 millilitre mark after a thumb lets go.
setup.caption: 3. Let go of the plunger. Watch what it does.

flow.do: Show your child the syringe. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will block the end of this syringe with clay, and push the plunger in. What do you think will happen when we let go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Block the end of a syringe. Push the plunger in. What happens when you let go? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A syringe with a plastic barrel and a rubber plunger works best. A bicycle pump with a thumb over the nozzle also works, but it has no millilitre marks, so push it halfway instead. With 2 to 4 children, one syringe is enough: take turns, and each child says what they felt. A second syringe lets two work in pairs.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Syringe Spring. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Pull the plunger out to 10 millilitres. 2. Press the nozzle firmly into the clay. 3. Push the plunger in slowly to 5 millilitres. 4. Feel the push back. 5. Let go and watch.
flow.say: Pull the plunger out to 10. Block the nozzle with clay. Push the plunger in slowly, to 5. What do you feel? Now let go.
flow.kid: Pull the plunger out to 10. Block the end with clay. Push the plunger in to 5. Feel the push back. Let go.

ask.q: What did the plunger do when you let go? Why?
good: It sprang back.
The air pushed it back.
The air was squashed and wanted more room.

flow.parent: The plunger should spring back to near 10. If it stays at 5, the clay plug leaks. Press the plug harder, or use a bigger lump of clay. The plunger may stop a little short of 10, because the rubber rubs on the barrel. That is fine. Squashed air pushes back because its tiny particles hit the walls more often when there is less room.
flow.context: In this step, you squash the air in the syringe and feel it push back.

flow.do: 1. Try to push the plunger in to 4 millilitres, but no further. 2. Notice how hard you have to push. 3. Let go, and watch.
flow.say: Try pushing the plunger in a bit further, to 4, but not past it. Is it harder or easier to push the last bit? What does that remind you of?
flow.kid: Push to 4. Not further. Is the last bit harder or easier? What does that remind you of?

ask.q: Is the last part of the push harder or easier than the first part? What does that remind you of?
good: Harder.
It is like pulling the rubber band further.
It pushes back more the more it is squashed.

flow.parent: Most children notice that the last part is harder, as with the band. Squashed air, like a stretched band, pushes back harder the more it is squeezed, so squashing it more stores more energy.

check.q: Why does the plunger spring back when you let go?
options: The squashed air stored energy and pushes the plunger out
Air is lighter than the plunger
The clay pushes the plunger
check.why: Squashing the air stored energy in it. When you let go, the air pushes back and gives the energy to the plunger. The clay only blocks the end. It does not push the plunger.

flow.context: In this step, you squash the air further and compare the push with the band.

flow.do: 1. Fill the syringe with water, pushing out all the air, and plug the nozzle with clay. 2. Try to push the plunger in. 3. Compare it with the air: which one could you squash?
flow.say: Now fill the syringe with water and block the end. Try to push the plunger in. Can you squash the water like the air? What is different?
flow.kid: Fill the syringe with water. Block the end. Try to push. Can you squash it like air?

ask.q: Can you squash the water as easily as the air? What does that tell you?
good: No, the water hardly moves.
Air can be squashed, water cannot.
Only the air can be a spring.

flow.parent: Do this over a tray or sink. Push gently, because the clay can pop out and squirt water. The plunger barely moves with water, while the air squashed to half. Air has room between its particles, so it can be squeezed, and then it pushes back. Water has hardly any room to squeeze.
flow.think: Why can air act as a spring when water cannot?
flow.context: In this step, you try the same push with water and see that only air can be squashed and push back.

projects.title: The Valley Track: can a marble climb higher than it started?

materials.item: a marble (goli) or a small steel ball

a strip of thin card about 100 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide, made from a cereal box or carton pieces joined end to end with tape, with both long edges folded up 1 centimetre to make a groove
masking tape
2 stacks of books or boxes, one about 20 centimetres high and the other that you can change
a ruler and a pencil
a box or towel to catch the marble

projects.safety: Keep marbles away from children under five, who may put them in their mouths. A grown-up should cut the card with scissors. Pick up stray marbles at once so nobody slips on them.

schedule.what: Build the valley track. Release the marble from 20 centimetres. Raise the far end bit by bit. Find the highest far end it can reach.

projects.record: A table with the height of the far end in centimetres, and whether the marble rolled out of the far end, stopped short, or just made it. Then write the highest far end that worked.
projects.context: In this project, you build a valley out of cardboard and release a marble from one side. You find out how high up the other side the marble can climb.

setup.art: A folded card strip bent into a valley, with its middle taped flat to the floor, its left end taped to a stack of books 20 centimetres high and the right end taped to a lower stack.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the middle of the strip flat to the floor. Tape one end to a stack 20 centimetres high and the other to a lower stack.

setup.art: A marble being released at the top of the left side of the valley with a flag marking 20 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Let the marble go from the 20 centimetre mark. It rolls down and up the far side.

setup.art: The right stack being raised book by book beside a ruler, and the marble stopping just short of the far end.
setup.caption: 3. Raise the far end bit by bit. Find the highest far end the marble can climb out of.

flow.do: Show your child the marble and the cardboard. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: A marble starts at the top of one side of a valley, 20 centimetres up. It rolls down and up the other side. How high can the other side be before the marble cannot climb out? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A marble rolls down a valley and up the far side. How high can the far side be? Why?

ask.q: Could the marble climb out if the far side were higher than the start? Why?
good: No, it started lower than that.
Yes, if it goes fast enough.
Only up to the same height.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children expect the marble to gain speed and go higher. Write the guess and reason. With 2 to 4 children, each writes a guess for the highest far end. Jobs: one releases, one watches the far end, one writes; swap after each setting.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Valley Track. You guess before you build.

flow.do: 1. Fold up both long edges of the card strip by 1 centimetre, to make a groove. 2. Lay the strip so its middle 10 centimetres lie flat on the floor, and tape them down. 3. Lift one end and tape it to the top of a stack of books 20 centimetres high. 4. Lift the other end and tape it to a stack 10 centimetres high. The strip now curves up on both sides, like a smile. 5. Put the catching box beyond the far end. 6. Roll the marble down once to test.
flow.say: Fold up the edges of the strip to make a groove. Tape the middle flat to the floor. Tape one end to the high stack and the other to the low stack, so it curves like a smile. Test with one roll.
flow.kid: Fold up the edges. Tape the middle to the floor. Tape one end high and one end low. Test one roll.
flow.parent: The groove must be smooth. Press out any wrinkle and keep the tape joins flat, because a bump takes energy. If the marble jumps out, fold the edges up higher. Measure the height of each end from the floor to the strip, at the end of the strip. If the strip bows up like a hill, press the middle down and tape it again.

check.q: Why do we always release the marble from the same mark at 20 centimetres?
options: So the start stays the same and only the far end changes
So the marble rolls faster
So the cardboard does not bend
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the start changed too, we would not know whether the start or the far end made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you build the valley the marble will roll through.

flow.do: 1. Set the far end at 10 centimetres and release the marble from the 20 centimetre mark. 2. Raise the far end by 2 centimetres at a time, to 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 and 22. 3. Each time, release the marble from the same start mark. 4. Write if it rolled out of the far end, stopped short, or just made it. 5. Last, set the far end at 26 centimetres and release the marble. A helper marks with a finger where it turns back. Measure that height.
flow.say: Set the far end low and release the marble. Raise the far end by 2 centimetres each time. Always start from the same mark. Write what the marble does each time. Last, put the far end high and mark where the marble turns back.
flow.kid: Raise the far end 2 centimetres at a time. Release from the same mark. Write what happens. Last, mark where it turns back.

ask.q: At what height does the marble stop being able to climb out?
good: Just below where it started.
A bit lower than the start.
About the same height as the start, but not quite.

flow.parent: A marble should climb out of a far end that is a little below the start, often within a few centimetres of it. But card, tape joins and wobble take energy, so yours may stop several centimetres short. No marble climbs out of a far end higher than the start. Try each setting twice, because one try can be a fluke. The turn-back mark is hard to see by eye, so film it on a phone if you can. If the marble stops far short even at the lowest setting, the track is bumpy: smooth the joins and press out the wrinkles.
flow.context: In this step, you raise the far end until the marble cannot climb out.

flow.do: 1. Write the highest far end that worked. 2. Compare it with the turn-back height from the last test. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think the marble could not climb higher than where it started?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: After your child has said what they saw, you can explain. At the start the marble held energy in its height. Rolling down turned it into movement, and climbing up turned it back into height. Some energy went into rubbing between the marble and the groove, and into the marble's spin and the track's wobble, as small amounts of heat and sound. So the marble reached a little less than its start, and never more. Energy cannot be made on the way.
flow.think: The marble stopped short of its start height. Where did the missing energy go?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Valley Track. You say what you found.

challenges.title: Beat the Drop: make a ball bounce higher than the place it was dropped from
challenges.problem: You have a big ball and a small bouncy ball. Find a way to make the small ball bounce higher than the height it was dropped from, using only the balls and your hands.
constraints: Use only the two balls and your hands. No throwing and no pushing down.
Let go from a height of 50 centimetres, with the top of the big ball at the 50 centimetre mark and the small ball resting on it.
Measure the highest point of the small ball's bounce on a tape stuck on the wall.
Do the test on a hard floor, in a room with a high ceiling and nothing breakable or glass nearby, away from fans.
materials: a big ball, such as a football or a rubber ball of about 20 centimetres (if you have none, use a cricket tennis ball underneath and a ping-pong ball or a very light small bouncy ball on top)
a small bouncy ball, such as a cricket tennis ball or a rubber ball
a tailor's tape or a metre stick stuck upright on a wall, with zero at the floor (a long tape of 150 centimetres or more helps)
a helper to read the bounce
general: Drop the small ball alone from 50 centimetres. It will bounce lower than 50 centimetres.
Use a very bouncy ball, such as a hard rubber ball, to get as close to 50 centimetres as possible.
Drop it onto a harder floor so less energy goes into the floor.
creative: Put the small ball on top of the big ball and drop them together. The small ball can shoot much higher than 50 centimetres.
Try the smallest and lightest ball on top, and the biggest and heaviest underneath.
Try three balls in a stack, with the lightest ball at the top.
challenges.your_turn: Try the stack. Try different balls. Which pair made the small ball bounce highest? Why do you think the small ball went higher than a single ball can?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about stores of energy. You try to make a ball bounce higher than the height it was dropped from.

setup.art: A small cricket tennis ball on its own being held at a flag on the wall and dropped to the floor, bouncing lower than the flag.
setup.caption: 1. Drop the small ball alone from the 50 centimetre flag. Note how high it bounces.

setup.art: A small ball resting on top of a bigger ball, both held at the 50 centimetre flag by a child's two hands.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the small ball centred on top of the big ball. Let go of both together.

setup.art: The small ball shooting up high past the flag on the wall, while the big ball stays low near the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Read how high the small ball goes. Try different balls.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child for ideas before trying anything, and write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: Can a ball bounce higher than the place it was dropped from? Think about it. What would a ball need to bounce that high? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Can a ball bounce higher than where it was dropped? What would it need? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Can a ball bounce higher than where it was dropped from? How?
good: No, it loses energy.
Yes, if something gives it extra energy.
Maybe with another ball.

flow.parent: Most children and many adults think it is impossible. That is a fair idea. A ball dropped alone cannot do it. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Beat the Drop. You plan.

flow.do: 1. Stick the tape on the wall, with zero at the floor. 2. Put a flag at 50 centimetres. 3. Drop the small ball alone from the flag, three times. 4. Write how high it bounces.
flow.say: Drop the small ball on its own from 50 centimetres. Your helper reads the bounce. Do it three times. This is the number we want to beat.
flow.kid: Drop the small ball alone from 50. The helper reads the bounce. Do it three times.
flow.parent: The small ball alone should bounce to about 25 to 40 centimetres, lower than the start. Use 50 centimetres for every test, so the results can be compared.
flow.context: In this step, you find the bounce of the small ball on its own.

flow.do: 1. Rest the small ball exactly on top of the big ball. 2. Hold them with the big ball's top at the 50 centimetre flag. 3. Let go of both at the same moment. 4. The helper reads the top of the small ball's bounce. 5. Try five times.
flow.say: Rest the small ball on top of the big ball. Hold them together at 50. Let go of both at the same moment. Your helper reads the small ball's bounce. Try five times.
flow.kid: Rest the small ball on top of the big ball. Hold them at 50. Let go of both together. Try five times.

ask.q: What did the small ball do compared with when it was dropped alone?
good: It went much higher.
It shot above the flag.
The big ball hardly bounced.

flow.parent: Stand clear. The small ball may fly sideways or hit the ceiling, so play where nothing can break and keep faces out of its path. Hold the big ball low on its sides with both hands, balance the small ball on top, and pull your hands away sideways at the same moment. A small wobble sends the small ball sideways, so it may take many tries. When the balls line up, the small ball often reaches about 1.5 to 3 times the start height; with a poor line-up, it may only do a little better or go sideways. Film it if you can. With 2 to 4 children, one drops, one steadies the tape and reads, one films, one writes; swap after each try. With one child, a parent reads the bounce.
flow.context: In this step, you drop the two balls together and watch what the small ball does.

flow.do: 1. Try other balls on top and underneath. 2. Write how high the top ball goes each time. 3. Find the pair that made the top ball bounce highest.
flow.say: Try other pairs of balls. Is it better with a bigger ball underneath? A lighter ball on top? Write the highest bounce for each pair.
flow.kid: Try other pairs. Write the highest bounce for each pair.
flow.parent: The bigger the difference in weight, with the heavy ball underneath and the light ball on top, the higher the small ball goes.
flow.context: In this step, you try different pairs of balls to find the best one.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain how the small ball could go higher than the place it was dropped from.
flow.say: Where did the extra energy come from? The small ball went higher than a single ball can. Why do you think the big ball hardly bounced?
flow.kid: Where did the small ball's extra energy come from? Why did the big ball hardly bounce?
flow.parent: After your child has said what they think, you can explain. Both balls started with energy of height. When the big ball hit the floor and began to rise, it hit the small ball, which was still falling. Most of the big ball's energy passed on to the small ball, and the big ball almost stopped. So the small ball got energy from the big ball. No energy was made. It was passed from one ball to the other.
flow.think: Did the two balls make new energy, or share the energy they had?
flow.context: This is the last step of Beat the Drop. You explain what you found.
