quiz.p: Which of these stores its energy in height?
quiz.why: Water in a roof tank is held high, and can fall. A banana is a chemical store, and a drawn bow is a stretch store.

quiz.p: What stops a stretched band from springing back at once?
quiz.why: Something holds it. A store waits while something holds it back, such as your fingers. Taking that away is the trigger.
opts: There is no energy in it

quiz.p: A good spring pulled back 3 centimetres makes a block slide 18 centimetres. About how far will it slide if pulled back 6 centimetres?
quiz.why: For a good spring, twice the pull-back stores about four times the energy, so the slide is about 4 times as far. 4 times 18 is 72 centimetres.

quiz.p: A ball dropped from 50 centimetres bounces to 30. About how high will it bounce if dropped from 100 centimetres?
quiz.why: Twice the height stores twice the energy, so the bounce is also about twice as high. 2 times 30 is 60.

quiz.p: Why does a bouncing ball rise less on each bounce?
quiz.why: A little of the ball's energy becomes heat and sound at each bounce. It is not destroyed, but it is too spread out to lift the ball again.
opts: Some energy becomes heat and sound each time
The Earth pulls harder each time

quiz.p: Where did the energy in the uranium of a nuclear power station first come from?
quiz.why: Uranium atoms were made in stars that exploded or collided, long before the Sun. So not every store begins with the Sun.

quiz.p: Which chain shows, in the right order, how energy reaches a hydro power station?
quiz.why: The Sun lifts water by evaporating it, rain brings it to the hills, and the dam holds it high. Falling water turns the turbine.
opts: The Sun, then evaporation, then rain on the hills, then the dam, then the turbine
The turbine, then the dam, then the Sun, then rain
The dam, then the Sun, then the turbine, then rain

quiz.p: The same ball is held in the same place. Once there is a table below it, and once there is only the floor. When is more energy stored?
quiz.why: With only the floor below, the ball can fall further and give back more energy. The energy depends on the ball and on what is below it.
opts: Both times the same, because it is the same ball

quiz.p: About how much energy is stored by lifting a small apple of 100 grams up by 1 metre?
quiz.why: That is about 1 joule, which is the unit of energy. Lifting 2 apples by 1 metre, or 1 apple by 2 metres, stores about 2 joules.

quiz.p: A trigger supplies the energy that comes out of a store.
quiz.why: False. A trigger only lets the stored energy out. A tiny match can release the huge chemical energy in a whole forest.

quiz.p: A cycle at 30 kilometres an hour has 9 times the movement energy of one at 10. About how many times as far does it need to stop?
quiz.why: Movement energy grows with the square of the speed. To stop, the brakes must take away 9 times as much energy, so it needs about 9 times the distance.

quiz.p: A friend says energy vanishes when a ball stops bouncing. What is the best reply?
quiz.why: The ball's energy became heat and sound that spread into the ball, the floor and the air. It is still in the world, but too spread out to use.
opts: It spread out as heat and sound, so it is still there
You are right, it is gone
It went back into the Sun

items.p: What is stored energy?
items.why: Stored energy is energy that waits in a thing because of its place, its shape or how its atoms are joined. It is not doing anything yet, but it can.
opts: Energy that waits in a thing, ready to be used later
Energy that a thing has used up

items.p: A ball is lifted twice as high as before. How much more energy is stored in its height?
items.why: The energy stored in height is the weight times the height. Twice the height stores twice the energy.

items.p: Sort each thing by the kind of store it uses.
items.why: Water in a tank and a coconut high on a palm hold energy in height. A wound spring, a drawn bow and squashed air hold it in a stretch or squash. A banana, a torch cell and firewood hold chemical energy.
items: a coconut on a tall palm
squashed air in a bicycle pump

items.p: The scientific name for stored energy is ____ energy.
items.why: Potential means able to happen. Potential energy is energy that is able to be used later.

items.p: A stretched rubber band holds energy even while you keep it still.
items.why: True. The energy waits in the stretch for as long as you hold it. Let go, and it comes out as movement.

items.p: Match each store to the trigger that lets its energy out.
items.why: A store waits while something holds it back. The trigger takes that away. A tap holds back the tank water, fingers hold back a bow string, and a switch holds back a cell.

items.p: What does a trigger do?
items.why: A trigger lets a store release its energy. It does not supply the energy. A tiny match can start a huge fire, because the energy comes from the wood.
opts: It removes what was holding the energy back
It adds the energy to the store

items.p: Lifting a small apple of about 100 grams up by 1 metre stores about 1 joule. How many joules are stored by lifting 5 such apples up by 2 metres?
items.why: Five apples store 5 times as much as one. Two metres stores twice as much as one metre. 5 times 2 is 10 joules.
items.why_maths: Weight and height both multiply the energy, so multiply them.

items.p: A friend wants to find out how far a band pushes a bar of soap. She changes the band and the pull-back every time. Why can she not tell what made the difference?
items.a: If two things change at once, she cannot tell which one caused the difference. She should change only the pull-back and keep the band the same.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. A strong answer says that two changes mix together, so the cause is hidden.

items.p: A ball dropped on its own can bounce higher than the place it was dropped from.
items.why: False. A ball loses a little energy as heat and sound at every bounce, so it rises less than it fell. It can rise higher only if something else gives it more energy.

items.p: Why does a bouncing ball rise less on every bounce?
items.why: A little of the ball's energy turns into heat and sound at each bounce and spreads out. It cannot be used to lift the ball again. The energy is not destroyed.
opts: A little energy turns into heat and sound each time
The ball gets lighter each time
The Earth pulls the ball harder each time

items.p: Energy stored in how atoms are joined, as in food and fuel, is called ____ energy.
items.why: Atoms in food and fuel are joined in patterns that hold energy. When they rearrange, the energy comes out.

items.p: Draw a ball bouncing three times, each bounce lower than the last. Mark where some of the energy goes each time the ball touches the floor.
items.a: A ball path with three bounces getting lower, and small wavy lines or arrows at the floor for heat and sound.
items.why: A strong drawing shows each bounce lower than the one before, and shows that the missing energy goes into heat and sound near the floor, not away from the world.

items.p: A banana gives you energy. Where did that energy first come from?
items.why: The banana plant built the fruit from sunlight, air and water. So the banana's energy was sunlight before it was fruit.
opts: Sunlight that the banana plant collected

items.p: You pull a rubber band back and hold it. What is holding the energy back, and what could be the trigger that lets it out?
items.a: Your fingers hold the band back. The trigger is letting go of the band.
items.why: A store waits while something holds it back. A strong answer names the thing that holds it, which is your fingers, and the trigger, which is letting go.

items.p: A good spring is stretched twice as far. About how many times as much energy is stored?
items.why: Twice the stretch means twice the pull at the end, over twice the distance. 2 times 2 is 4. For a good spring, the energy grows with the stretch multiplied by itself.

items.p: A good spring stores 3 joules when it is stretched 1 centimetre. About how many joules does it store when stretched 3 centimetres?
items.why: Stretch 3 times as far, and the energy grows 3 times 3, which is 9 times. 9 times 3 joules is 27 joules.
items.why_maths: Energy in a spring grows with the square of the stretch, so square the number first.

items.p: Lifting a thing twice as heavy to the same height stores twice as much energy.
items.why: True. The energy stored in height is the weight times the height. Twice the weight stores twice the energy.

items.p: Here are two views about a ball held above a table.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and uses the fact that the same ball over the floor gives back more.
items.why: Both views describe the numbers correctly. The second view shows why the numbers change when the floor changes, so physicists often prefer it.

views.says: The ball has the energy. It is a property of the ball, like its weight.
The ball and the Earth share the energy. Over a table the ball can fall less, so the pair stores less.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What test could help you decide?

items.p: Here is a drawing of a ball just after it is let go, just before it hits the floor, and squashed against the floor. Label each moment with the store that holds most of the energy.
items.why: At the top, the ball holds its energy in height. Just before it lands, the energy is movement. At the floor, the ball is squashed and holds it as a squash, like a spring.
labels: A: the ball held still at the top
B: the ball just before it hits the floor
C: the ball squashed on the floor
items.art: Three pictures of a ball: held high above a floor, just above the floor with speed lines, and flattened against the floor.

items.p: Here are made-up results from a test that hangs water from a rubber band. What does the straight line show?
items.why: A straight line through the dots means that the stretch grows in step with the weight. Twice the weight gives about twice the stretch, so the band pulls back twice as hard when stretched twice as far.
opts: Twice the weight gives about twice the stretch
The band stretches the same for any weight
The band stretches less for each extra weight

items.p: Ball A is dropped from 80 centimetres and bounces to 50 centimetres. Ball B is dropped from 80 centimetres and bounces to 60 centimetres. How many more centimetres does ball B bounce than ball A?
items.why: 60 take away 50 is 10. Ball B keeps more of its energy at each bounce, so its bounce is 10 centimetres higher.
items.why_maths: Subtracting two bounce heights shows which ball gives back more of its energy.

items.p: Put these steps of a hydro power station in order, from the beginning: the turbine spins, rain falls on the hills, the bulb lights, the Sun heats the sea, water falls from the dam, water evaporates.
items.why: The Sun heats the sea so water evaporates. It falls as rain on the hills and is held in the dam. When it falls, it turns the turbine, which makes the electricity for the bulb.

items.p: A cycle moves at 20 kilometres an hour, and then at 10. How much movement energy does it have at 20 compared with 10?
items.why: Movement energy grows with the square of the speed. Twice the speed has 2 times 2, which is 4 times the energy.

items.p: In a bounce test, a ball dropped from 30 centimetres bounces to 20. Dropped from 60, it bounces to 41. Dropped from 90, it bounces to 58. Describe the pattern, and predict the bounce from 120 centimetres.
items.a: The bounce is about two thirds of the drop each time. From 120 centimetres, the bounce should be about 80 centimetres.
items.why: A strong answer notices that the bounce is a steady fraction of the drop height, about two thirds, and uses it. 2/3 of 120 is 80.

items.p: A banana holds about 420 000 joules. A full 1000 litre roof tank 10 metres up holds about 98 000 joules. Which holds more, and about how many times more?
items.why: 420 000 divided by 98 000 is a little more than 4. The banana holds more, because chemical stores hold far more energy for their size than a store of height.
opts: The banana, by about four times
The tank, by about four times

items.p: A pumped storage dam uses 100 units of electricity to pump water up and gets back 75 units. Where did the other 25 units go, and are they destroyed?
items.a: They turned into heat in the pumps, pipes and turbines. They were not destroyed. The heat spread out and cannot be used again.
items.why: A strong answer says the energy became spread-out heat and is not destroyed, using the idea that energy is never lost but can become too spread out to use.

items.p: When a ball stops bouncing, its energy has vanished from the world.
items.why: False. The energy has become heat and sound that spread into the ball, the floor and the air. It is still in the world, but too spread out to lift the ball again.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Coal, petrol, wood, uranium.
items.a: Uranium, because its energy was made in stars, not by the Sun. Coal, petrol and wood hold sunlight.
items.why: Coal, petrol and wood come from plants and sea life that were built from sunlight. Uranium atoms were made in exploding stars long before the Sun.

items.p: Another name for movement energy is ____ energy.
items.why: Kinetic comes from a Greek word for movement. Kinetic energy is the energy of anything that is moving.

items.p: Food holds far more energy than the same weight of water lifted high, yet some cities store electricity as water held on a hill. Why might they choose water?
items.a: A water store can be filled and emptied thousands of times, quickly, with little loss. Chemical stores in food cannot be refilled quickly or turned into electricity easily.
items.why: A strong answer notices that a good store is not only about size. How fast it can be filled and emptied, how often, and how much comes back also matter.

items.p: A state wants to build a pumped storage dam in a hill forest, so the city's lights stay on at night.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and says what else could be done.
items.why: Both views are reasonable. A good answer weighs the energy stored against the forest, and asks whether another place or kind of store could do the job.

views.who: Someone who works at the power company (an imagined view)
views.says: The dam stores cheap daytime energy for the evening and keeps the city's hospitals and schools running. It is worth building.

views.who: Someone who studies forest birds (an imagined view)
views.says: The dam would flood the homes of hundreds of living beings. We should store energy in batteries or in a place that is already damaged.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you want to know before you decided?

items.p: Which of these energy stores did NOT begin as sunlight?
items.why: The energy in uranium was made in exploding and colliding stars, long before the Sun was born. Wind, dosa and petrol all came from the Sun.

items.p: A full tank of 1000 litres lifted 10 metres holds about 98 000 joules. If the same tank were lifted 20 metres, how many joules would it hold?
items.why: Twice the height stores twice the energy. 98 000 times 2 is 196 000 joules.
items.why_maths: Doubling the height doubles the energy, so double the number.

items.p: A friend says a ball must store the same energy wherever you lift it from, because it is the same ball. Use the idea of falling to answer her.
items.a: The energy depends on how far the ball can fall. The same ball held over a floor can fall further than over a table, so it stores more.
items.why: A strong answer says that stored energy depends on the ball and on what is below it. Over a table, the ball has less far to fall than over the floor.

items.p: Draw an energy chain from the Sun to a child kicking a football. Label each store along the way.
items.a: The Sun, then a plant, then food, then the child's muscles, then the football's movement.
items.why: A strong chain starts at the Sun and has at least four links: light, sugar in the plant, food in the child, and movement. Heat should be shown leaving at each step.

items.p: A tiny match can start a forest fire. What does this tell you about a trigger?
items.why: A trigger only lets the store out. The huge energy comes from the stored chemical energy of the trees, not from the match.
opts: The trigger can be tiny, because the energy comes from the store
The match holds as much energy as the forest
Fires start only in dry forests

items.p: In a pumped storage dam, all the electricity used to pump the water uphill comes back.
items.why: False. About three-quarters comes back. The rest turns into heat in the pumps, pipes and turbines.

items.p: Here are made-up bounce results. About what fraction of the drop height does the ball keep each time?
items.why: 30 to 20, 60 to 40 and 90 to 60 are all two thirds. A steady fraction means each bounce keeps about the same share of the energy.

items.p: Match each living or non-living store to the kind of energy it holds.
items.why: A tendon stretches and springs back, like a band. Fat is a chemical store. Water behind a dam holds energy in height. Compressed air in a tyre is a squash store.
pairs: The tendon at the back of your heel
Air squashed in a bicycle tyre

items.p: A small ball on top of a big ball can bounce higher than the height it was dropped from. Is energy being made? Explain.
items.a: No. The big ball passes most of its energy on to the small ball. The big ball almost stops, and the small ball goes higher. The total energy stays the same.
items.why: A strong answer says that the energy moves from the big ball to the small ball, and the total stays the same. A ball on its own cannot do this.

items.p: Sort each store by where its energy began.
items.why: Rice, wind, rain in a dam and firewood all trace back to the Sun. Uranium comes from old stars, the tide from the Moon's pull, and a hot spring from heat inside the Earth.

items.p: A cycle stops in 2 metres when it is going 10 kilometres an hour. Going 4 times as fast needs 16 times the distance to stop. How many metres is that?
items.why: 16 times 2 metres is 32 metres. Four times the speed gives 4 times 4, which is 16 times the movement energy to get rid of.
items.why_maths: Square numbers show how quickly stopping gets harder as speed goes up.

items.p: Einstein's equation says that every gram of matter is equal to about ____ trillion joules.
items.why: One gram times the speed of light squared is about 90 trillion joules. Almost all of it stays locked up in ordinary matter.

items.p: The energy of a hot cup of chai that cools is spread into the air and is not destroyed.
items.why: True. The heat spreads into the cup and the air. It is still in the world, but too spread out to be of use.

applications: Roof water tanks and dams store energy in height, for water and for electricity.
Pumped storage power stations such as Kadamparai store electricity as water held high.
Rechargeable batteries in phones, torches and electric scooters store chemical energy.
Springs in pens, door closers, clocks and the seats of cycles store energy in a squash or a twist.
Bows, catapults and the ropes of a swing use energy stored in stretch and in height.
Food, cooking gas and firewood store chemical energy that we release as heat and movement.
Speed limits near schools, because movement energy grows with the square of the speed.
Tendons in your legs store and give back energy as you run, like springs.
Bumpers and crumple zones in vehicles take in the movement energy of a crash.
The idea of fat as a store explains how birds, camels and bears survive long journeys or hard seasons.

open_questions.q: Where exactly is the energy of a lifted ball or a pulled-back band?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists agree on the numbers, but they disagree on whether the energy sits in the objects, in the field between them, or nowhere in particular. In Einstein's theory of gravity, nobody has found an agreed way to say where gravity's energy is.

open_questions.q: Could the total energy of the whole universe be exactly zero?
open_questions.why_open: In 1973 Edward Tryon suggested that the energy of all matter might be cancelled by the negative energy of gravity. This is an idea that some physicists like and others doubt. Nobody has found a way to test it.

open_questions.q: How can we store the summer Sun for the winter, cheaply and for months?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries and pumped storage work well for hours and days, but storing large amounts of energy across seasons is still an unsolved problem.

open_questions.q: What is the energy of empty space, which scientists call dark energy?
open_questions.why_open: Measurements of far galaxies suggest that most of the energy in the universe is of a kind no one has explained. It may be the biggest store of all.

open_questions.q: Could we make a battery as light and as long-lasting as fat?
open_questions.why_open: Fat stores about 40 times more energy in each kilogram than a phone battery does. Nobody has made a battery that comes close.

maths.problem: In a made-up Soap Slider test, a pull-back of 2 centimetres made the soap slide 10 centimetres. A pull-back of 4 centimetres made it slide 40 centimetres, and 6 centimetres made it slide 90 centimetres. How many times as far did it slide when the pull-back doubled from 2 to 4? If the pattern goes on, how far would a pull-back of 8 centimetres slide the soap?
maths.explain: 40 divided by 10 is 4. So doubling the pull-back made the slide 4 times as far. The slides are 10 times 1, 10 times 4 and 10 times 9. Here 1 is 1 times 1, 4 is 2 times 2 and 9 is 3 times 3. A pull-back of 8 centimetres is the fourth step, so the number is 4 times 4, which is 16. 10 times 16 is 160. A real band stops following the pattern if it is stretched too far.
maths.context: This is about the Soap Slider test, where you pulled a band back different distances. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in your results lets you predict a result you have not measured, which is what scientists do.

maths.problem: In the Bounce Ratio test, a ball dropped from 90 centimetres bounced back to 60 centimetres. What fraction of the drop height came back? If every bounce keeps the same fraction, how high is the second bounce?
maths.answer: 2/3 came back. The second bounce is 40 centimetres.
maths.explain: 60 out of 90 is 2/3, because 60 is 2 lots of 30 and 90 is 3 lots of 30. The second bounce keeps 2/3 of 60. A third of 60 is 20, so two thirds is 40.
maths.context: This is about the Bounce Ratio test, where you dropped a ball from different heights. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how much of the energy comes back at every bounce, however high you drop the ball.

maths.problem: Lifting a small apple of 100 grams up by 1 metre stores about 1 joule. How many joules are stored by lifting 3 such apples up by 4 metres?
maths.explain: One apple lifted 1 metre stores 1 joule. Three apples is 3 times as much, and 4 metres is 4 times as much. 3 times 4 is 12.
maths.context: This is about energy stored in height. One joule is about what it takes to lift a small apple up by 1 metre.
maths.why_maths: Weight and height both multiply the stored energy, so multiplying them gives the answer.

maths.problem: A full roof tank of 1000 litres lifted 10 metres holds about 98 000 joules. A full phone battery holds about 54 000 joules. About how many phone batteries is the tank worth?
maths.explain: 98 000 is close to 100 000. 54 000 is close to 50 000. 100 000 divided by 50 000 is 2. The exact figure is a little below 2, because 98 000 divided by 54 000 is about 1.8.
maths.context: A roof tank is a store of height, and a phone battery is a chemical store. This compares them.
maths.why_maths: Rounding to easy numbers lets you compare two big stores quickly in your head.

maths.problem: A banana holds about 420 000 joules. Lifting a small apple up by 1 metre stores about 1 joule. How many kilometres high would you have to lift the apple to store as much as the banana?
maths.explain: Each metre of lift stores 1 joule, so 420 000 joules needs 420 000 metres. There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. 420 000 divided by 1000 is 420 kilometres.
maths.context: Chemical stores in food are huge compared with stores of height. This puts the banana in metres and kilometres.
maths.why_maths: Changing metres into kilometres makes a very big number easy to picture.

maths.problem: In a made-up Hanging Water test, a band stretched 0 centimetres with no water, 1 centimetre with 100 millilitres, 2 centimetres with 200 millilitres and 3 centimetres with 300 millilitres. How much would it stretch with 500 millilitres, if the pattern keeps going? Why should you not trust that for a very heavy load?
maths.answer: 5 centimetres. A band stops following the pattern when it is stretched very far.
maths.explain: Each 100 millilitres adds 1 centimetre, so 500 millilitres adds 5. A real band stretches less for each extra 100 millilitres at the end, and it may snap, so a pattern is only good inside the range you tested.
maths.context: This is about the Hanging Water activity, where you hung water from a band and measured how far it stretched. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: A line graph that goes straight lets you predict, but only inside the range you measured.

maths.problem: A pumped storage dam uses 100 units of electricity to pump water uphill, and gives back 75 units when the water runs down. What fraction of the energy is lost? What happens to it?
maths.explain: 100 take away 75 is 25. 25 out of 100 is 1/4. The 25 units turned into heat in the pumps, pipes and turbines. The heat spreads into the air and cannot be used to make electricity again.
maths.context: A pumped storage dam is a big store of height. It does not give back all the energy it was given.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how good a store is at giving energy back.

maths.problem: A cycle going 10 kilometres an hour stops in about 2 metres. Going twice as fast needs 4 times the distance to stop. How far does the cycle need to stop at 20 kilometres an hour? At 30 kilometres an hour, which is 3 times as fast, it needs 9 times the distance. How far is that?
maths.answer: 8 metres at 20 kilometres an hour. 18 metres at 30 kilometres an hour.
maths.explain: At 20, the distance is 4 times 2, which is 8 metres. At 30, the distance is 9 times 2, which is 18 metres. Movement energy grows with the square of the speed.
maths.context: Movement energy grows faster than speed. Twice the speed has four times the energy, so a cycle needs four times the distance to stop.
maths.why_maths: Square numbers explain why speed limits matter so much near schools.

roots.context: We have measured stores of stretch and height, and followed their energy back to the Sun. Now we ask what a store really is, and what that tells us about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Hold a ball 30 centimetres above a table, and it can give back a little. Take the table away, and the same ball in the same place can give back much more. So the energy is not stored in the ball alone. It is stored between the ball and what it can fall towards.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'this ball has so much energy' as if the number were printed on the ball, like its colour or its weight. But the number changes when the floor changes. Stored energy is always about a thing and something else.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Table or Floor test, the ball was held in exactly the same place. Over the stool, its bounce was small. Over the floor, it bounced much higher. If your own numbers differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: Your body is a store. Fat, sugar and the stretch in your tendons hold energy that you spend when you choose. What you can do depends on what you are holding in reserve.
three.what_is_life: A seed holds a first meal for a plant. A bird holds fat for a long flight. Living beings store energy so that they can act later, when food is not there.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of stores of height, stretch, chemicals and matter. Energy is rarely made or lost. It mostly moves from one store to another.

roots.thread: A store looks like a single thing, but it always has two parts that are held apart. The ball and the Earth are held apart. The atoms in a stretched band are pulled out of line. In food, the sugar and the oxygen are kept from joining. When the two parts come together again, the energy comes out as movement, and then as heat. Some physicists think that, in the whole universe, all the stores might add up to exactly zero. That is an idea, and nobody knows for sure.

teachings.teaching: That is whole, and this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: When a store lets its energy out, the world's total stays exactly the same. The whole remains whole.

teachings.teaching: The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows. It is empty, yet it gives and never runs dry. The more it moves, the more it gives.
teachings.link: The energy of a lifted ball is held in the gap between the ball and the Earth, in the empty-looking space between them.

teachings.link: A ball's stored energy needs the whole Earth below it. No store belongs to one thing alone.

science.text: Energy is never made or lost. It moves between stores, and some of it spreads out as heat.
Some physicists think the total energy of the whole universe might be exactly zero, because the energy of matter is cancelled by gravity. Edward Tryon suggested it in 1973.

other_view.view: It is fine to say the ball has potential energy. Everyone gets the same numbers, so where the energy sits is only a way of talking. The question has no use.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the listed things. Soap Slider: the two pencils stand in clay 10 centimetres apart, and the soap leaves the band when the band is straight again, so the slide can be measured cleanly. A soap of 75 to 100 grams on tiles may slide only a few centimetres from a 2 centimetre pull-back and far more from 6. Bands differ a lot, so the steps say what to do when the soap barely moves or flies far. Twice the pull-back should give more than twice the slide, often 3 to 10 times, but this needs a home test. The V shape of the band adds to the effect, which the parent note says. Hanging Water needs a thick band, and the stretch for each 100 millilitres is often a little smaller near 400, so the graph may curve slightly. Bounce Ratio: most balls return half to two thirds of the drop height, and the fraction is steady. A bounce is quick, so the steps suggest a phone in slow motion. Table or Floor: the bounce above the floor should be about 2 to 3 times the bounce above the stool. Beat the Drop (the stacked balls) takes a few tries and can send the small ball sideways, so it is marked for a grown-up and says to play where nothing can break. The Valley Track marble should climb out of far ends a little below the start height, and never above it. Hanging Water and the Syringe Spring were checked for safety only, and need a home test for the numbers. how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1700s, scientists argued about how to measure the force of a moving ball. Most followers of Descartes and Newton said it was the mass times the speed. So a ball moving twice as fast should hit twice as hard. In the early 1720s, the Dutch professor Willem 's Gravesande dropped brass balls into soft clay from different heights. A ball that hit twice as fast made a dent four times as deep. The French scientist Émilie du Châtelet read about his clay tests and was convinced. In the early 1740s, in her book Institutions de Physique, she argued that the force of motion grows with the square of the speed, as the philosopher Leibniz had said. Some members of the French Academy argued against her. Over the next century her side won, and today movement energy is half the mass times the speed squared. She also translated Newton's Principia into French, and her translation is still read.
how_we_found_out.who: Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch professor, and Émilie du Châtelet, a French scientist and translator
how_we_found_out.when: The early 1720s for the clay tests, and the early 1740s for her book
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought that a moving body's force was simply its mass times its speed, so twice the speed would give twice the dent. The clay showed four times the dent for twice the speed.

A rubber band pulled back twice as far stores only twice the energy.

A ball that has stopped bouncing has lost its energy for ever.
Energy is never destroyed. It has spread out as heat and sound in the ball, the floor and the air.

Movement energy grows faster than speed. Twice the speed digs a dent about four times as deep.
A single ball dropped alone can bounce higher than the place it fell from.
Every bounce loses a little energy as heat and sound, so the ball cannot rise above where it started.
Almost all the energy in food, fuel and wind began as sunlight.
Plants catch sunlight to make food and fuel, and the Sun's heat moves the air to make wind.
A machine can be built that gives out more energy than it takes in.
